maintopic: SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO INQUIRE INTO QUESTIONS CONCERNING RETURNED MEN AND DEPENDANTS
speechtext:
A special committee was
appointed yesterday to consider problems affecting returned soldiers. The number comprising the committee was fixed at seventeen. Apparently seventeen is an infraction of the rule, which would limit the number to fifteen. 1 move, therefore:
That the provision of standing order No. 65, under which no special committee may, without leave of the house, consist of more than fifteen members, be suspended in connection with the resolution passed by this house on February 15, appointing the special committee on pensions and returned soldiers' problems.
Motion agreed to.

I desire to direct attention to an entirely misleading, I may say, false, statement, with reference to what I said the other day during the debate on national banking, which is contained in the Toronto Evening Telegram of February 14 in what purports to be an account of the proceedings of that date, despatched by the special staff correspondent. I find that under the guise of a report a vicious attack on myself. Under the special heading " Rebellion Suggested " I read:
But his language grew stronger as he went along, and he pictured the whole of the national credit drifting into the hands of two or three men and then recorded his sad conviction that, "If anything would justify armed rebellion against the established condition of affairs, I think such conservation of the banking system is the one thing that would justify it."
Strange, isn't it, how these peaceful little chaps-most of them pacifists-are always ready to talk red rebellion. Makes you wonder, if said rebellion ever did come, whether they'd fight or raise wheat to feed the fighters.
All that I said in this connection will be found recorded in Hansard' at page 389.
Some hon. gentlemen may remember a rather remarkable statement made during the election of 1925 by Sir Clifford Sifton. He said:
"We are rapidly approaching that condition in which two or at most three banks will be doing the whole of the business of the Dominion and you will have the spectacle of about three men sitting on the whole of the funds of the people of Canada deposited in the banks and deciding to whom they will loan these funds." And again:
"If anything would justify an armed rebellion against the established condition of affairs I

Mr. Speaker, by unanimous consent between

The Budget-Mr. Robh
the leaders of the different parties, which we on this side appreciate very much, I move:
That Mr. Speaker do now leave the chair for the house to go into committee of ways and means.
Mr. Speaker, seldom have the annual statements from leaders of finance and industry throughout Canada so generally reflected such progress and prosperity as that of the year 1927; and the statement of the nation's business,' which to-day I have the honour to present, will show conclusively that, notwithstanding our annual reductions in the rate of taxation, our revenues have been ample to meet fixed charges, take care of the ever increasing needs of a growing country, and provide also for a reduction of debt.
Public Accounts 1926-27
In the budget speech of February 17, 1927, it was estimated that the net debt would be reduced by some $31,366,000. The public accounts recently tabled show that the net debt was actually reduced by $41,896,729.33, or some $10,500,000 more than estimated. This was due to the practice which has always been followed when estimating revenues and expenditures.
That there should be no uncertainty as to the correctness of the public accounts of this Dominion, I recommended to the treasury board that an independent audit be made of the balance sheet of the public accounts as of March 31, 1924, 1925, 1926 and 1927. The well-known firm of chartered accountants, P. S. Ross & Sons, of Montreal, Toronto and Winnipeg, were engaged and instructed to make a complete audit of the departmental accounts in question, and on the fifth of December last their certificate which is printed on page xiv of the public accounts for the year 1926-27, was received. Their report confirms the accuracy of the public accounts as submitted to parliament and certified that the reduction in the net debt during the period in question was $105,942,498.65.

Net Debt Reduced $38,815,000 After provision has been made to the extent of $16,000,000 for the writing down of certain soldier land settlement loans and other assets, the reduction in the net debt will be

S38 815,000. Thus, during the five-year period ending 31st March, 1928, after providing for writing down certain assets, we will have succeeded in reducing our net debt by $144,700.000. „ , , Chapter 68 of the statutes of 1927 amended the Soldier Land Settlement Act of 1919, and provided for the revaluation of loans to settlers for the purchase of lands. The soldier settlement board advise the Department of Finance that the total amount likely to be written off through this revaluation will be about $8,000,000. We propose reducing our assets as shown in the public accounts at the close of the present year by this sum of- $8,000,000. The soldier settlement board also advise that there will be a further loss on the re-sale of stock and equipment, as well as on farms which have reverted to the board. Certain of these farms have been resold, but some 3,000 properties remain to be disposed of. In the opinion of the board a loss will eventually be sustained in connection with the assets referred to of approximately $6,000,000 which sum the government proposes to write off as a non-active asset.
It has also been deemed advisable to reduce by some $2,000,000 active assets now carried as seed grain and relief advances, transferring this amount to non-active assets. These accounts have been running for many years and a certain number are now considered of doubtful value.
Outstanding Public Debt. Representations have been made in this house and elsewhere that, through a sinking fund properly invested, provision should be made for retirement of our total debt within a limited number of years. I do not intend to go into the merits of this proposal beyond remarking that there are opinions both for and against the adoption of a fixed plan. In the final analysis it must be recognized that a net surplus of revenues over all expenditures is the only effectual sinking fund for debt retirement. In 1845 an eminent British economist, McCulloch, dealing with the question of sinking funds and taxation, declared:
The greater productiveness of industry and the greater well_being of the community are the real sinking funds which a wise government should exert itself to build up and encourage.
In recent years we Canadians have succeeded in reducing annually both debt and taxation; each reduction of interest bearing debt has enabled us to reduce taxation further, and while welcoming any workable plan that will ensure the retirement of our national debt, I submit that until Canada is nearer
The Budget-Mr. Robb
the pre-war rate of taxation, annual reduction of taxes is as important as reduction of debt. Our policy is to reduce both.
Retirement of Maturing Loans
Mr. Speaker, total maturities for the current fiscal year, amounting to $100,505,650, were provided for as follows:
On the 1st and 15th November, 1927, the 5^ per cent renewal loan of 1922 amounting to $29,068,400, and the 3-year 4 per cent notes amounting to $8,000,000 matured and were redeemed in cash.	_
On the 1st December, 1927, a portion of the 54 per cent 1917 victory loan, tax-free, amounting to $63,437,250 matured. We were able to redeem $18,437,250 in cash. To meet the balance we issued 4 per cent 3-year treasury notes to the amount of $45,000,000 which we sold direct to the chartered banks of Canada at par. All of the chartered banks subscribed to this issue. The sale of these treasury notes marks the first financing since 1912 which the Dominion government has effected at a net cost as low as 4 per cent.
The saving in interest resulting from these transactions will be $3,607,000 annually. An additional advantage will accrue from a further reduction in the amount of outstanding tax-free bonds, as the December 1st maturity of $63,437,250 carried exemption from taxation.

This issue was made to provide for the following authorized commitments of the railway company:

Parliament last year authorized the government to guarantee securities of the Canadian National (West Indies) Steamships Limited to provide for the construction of steamships for the West Indies service. A guarantee to the amount of $8,000,000 has been executed but actual borrowing will take place only to meet cash requirements as construction proceeds. The company has arranged for bank advances as collateral for which the guaranteed securities are to be pledged.
The international trade of Canada is well maintained. Our fiscal year does not end for some weeks but the records for the nine months ended December 31, indicate a substantial favourable balance. This is particularly note-worthy at a time when industrial expansion and undertakings of various natures create a demand for machinery, construction material and other necessary articles not procurable in Canada. Imports of necessary supplies of raw materials for further manufacture are also on a larger scale. As we look back to the years when railways were being extended across the Dominion and western Canada was being settled, it will be recalled that there were annual unfavourable balances of trade, the adverse balance in the calendar year 1913 being $222,000,000, one of the highest in our history.
The League of Nations in 1927 made an interesting comparison of the international trade of the world and for this purpose took the calendar years 1913 and 1926. It was 
found that in 1913 only three nations had favourable trade balances. In that year the United States had a favourable trade balance of $7.13 per capita, Argentine $6.78 per capita, and British India 60 cents per capita. Thirteen years later there were six countries with favourable balances of trade, and Canada, which in 1913 had an unfavourable balance of $29.61 per capita, in 1926 led the world with a favourable balance of $29.34 per head of population. Trade With Treaty Countries
Favoured nation treatment is of importance alike to basic producers and to manufacturers of finished products. Our prolonged winters tend to restrict employment in some industries while others have only a short marketing season in Canada. Consequently, to maintain a high state of efficiency, ex-

The Budget-Mr. Robb
port markets are to many industries, as well as to basic producers, of almost primary importance. Canada now enjoys favourable trade relations with many foreign countries to whom we sold $157,000,000 of goods in the fiscal year 1927, purchasing in return $78,000,000. '
Empire Trade
Our trade records show that in the fiscal year 1927 we sold to the empire goods to the value of $542,000,000 and purchased in return $214,000,000, collecting in duties from these imports $36,598,000. Sometimes comparisons are made to arrive at the average rates of duties assessed under various columns, so it may be pointed out in passing that nearly 35 per cent of the total duties collected on empire imports was paid on $25,711,000 of alcoholic beverages. If we except the United Kingdom from the calculations it will be noted that in the fiscal year 1927 Canada purchased from other British countries goods to the value of about $50,000,000. On these imports $4,267,000 were collected in customs, over 54 per cent of the total being paid as duties on sugar and spirits, thus showing in a broad way that the major portion of our imports from the British dominions and possessions consists of non-competitive and raw products. As practically all of our $94,000,000 of exports to those British dominions and possessions are fully manufactured, the value of working for closer trade relations within the empire is surely apparent.
Reductions in Taxes
Provision having been made for expected expenditures in the coming fiscal year and heed taken to maturing obligations, it is with pleasure and satisfaction that once again we are in a position to propose further reductions in taxation. As an added encouragement to business, as a measure of relief to taxpayers and to those provinces where local income taxes are levied, it is proposed that the Dominion shall continue gradually to lighten the load in the income tax field. Last year a reduction of ten per cent in all 'ates of the income tax was announced. To-day we are able to go a step further and to propose that the income tax payable by individuals be reduced an additional ten per cent. The list of exemptions is to be increased by allowing an exemption of $500 to those supporting dependents over twenty-one years of age who are incapable of self-support on account of mental or physical infirmity. In the case of corporations and joint stock companies, it is proposed that the tax be eight per cent net.
A general reduction of twenty-five per cent will be made in the sales tax.
The Customs Tariff
We come now to the customs tariff. The Advisory Board on Tariff and Taxation has concluded its hearings in respect of the textile group, excepting silk and artificial silk, and in the proposed revision there will be shown a general reduction in rates.
Cottons
Considering first the items comprising the cotton schedule, it is proposed that the maximum under the general tariff be reduced from 374 per cent to 30 per cent with a single exception.
On a large range of household cottons, and also on cotton socks and stockings, cotton underwear and cotton clothing, the rates will be materially reduced.
Coupled with the general lowering of rates on the finished products is a lowering of rates on yams and other materials used by the manufacturers for further processes. In the proposed changes the needs of the Canadian consumer and manufacturer have been carefully considered, while incidentally the scope of the British preference has been materially widened.
Woollens
In revising the woollen schedules two main considerations have been kept in mind, the vital necessity for warm clothing in a climate such as ours, and the position of the Canadian mills which weave woollen and worsted cloths. It is proposed to aid the Canadian weaving industry by granting free yarns for weaving purposes. The importations of woollen and worsted yarns are large, and the concession proposed should be of material assistance to the industry.
The drawback of duty on dry spun yams will be abolished on October 1, 1928.
Material decreases in duty will be made in the preferential rate on woollen goodg imported in the gray for dyeing and finishing in Canada.
There will be a reduction in the duty on all mitts and on all but the more expensive lines of woollen underwear, socks and stockings. A reduction is also proposed on certain woollen fabrics.
Linen, Flax and Jute Products The classification of linens and of flax and jute products will be separated from that of cottons. The linen schedules now proposed will conform in structure to those relating to cottons and wollens.
In respect to the finer grades of linens, which are not produced in Canada, there will be reductions in the British preferential rates.
The Budget-Mr. Robb

Silk and Artificial Silk
Practically no changes in rates are made in the silk or artificial silk items, as hearings on these groups have not been completed; but the wording of the schedules has been revised to conform to that of the cotton, woollen and linen schedules.
Textile Machinery
As a further assistance to the textile industry, the duty on machinery incidental to the working-up of fibrous materials will be adjusted. This machinery is now entered under items 467 and 468. The Department of National Revenue find difficulty in administering these items, as one overlaps the other. It is considered advisable to merge the two items into one. The new item may result in an increase in the duty on a small portion of the imports if such imports enter under the general tariff, but the reduction under the British preferential and the intermediate tariffs will more than offset that increase. On a small part of the machinery imported under the first item there will be no change, but on a large part of the importations a reduction is proposed from ten per cent to free under the British preferential tariff and from ten per cent to five per cent under the intermediate tariff.
Other Tariff Changes
The duty on machinery for mining and concentration of ores will be reduced. This reduction applies to locomotives for underground haulage in mining, to mine hoists of a class or kind not made in Canada, and to parts of certain mining machinery. It is proposed to make the duty on press blankets of a class or kind not made in Canada free under the British preferential tariff, five per cent under the intermediate tariff, and ten per cent under the general tariff. At present the imports of these blankets come in under the general tariff, the rates ranging from twenty to thirty-five per cent under different items.
It is proposed to reduce certain paper mill wrappings from fifteen to five per cent, British preferential tariff, and from twenty-five to ten per cent under the general tariff.
Flake calcium chloride, for road-treating purposes only, is placed on the free list.
It is proposed to make free under all tariffs non-alcoholic preparations or chemicals for disinfecting, dipping or spraying.
Crude petroleum, not in its natural state, imported for refining purposes, is made free under all tariffs until July 1, 1931.
The tariff rate on engines for fishing boats is now fifteen per cent under the general tariff. It is proposed that the parts therefor shall enter at the same rate. This is a reduction of twelve and a half per cent.
The present rates covering engines, and complete parts, for equipment of aircraft, are to be extended until July 1, 1930.
It is proposed to place on the free list under all tariffs nickel chromium, in bars or rods, of a class or kind not made in Canada, for use in the manufacture of electric resistance wire.
Drawbacks
Assistance is given the publishing industry by granting a drawback of 80 per cent on certain papers used in the production of magazines.
A drawback of 99 per cent is granted on bituminous coal used in melting or evaporating salt produced in Canada.
A drawback of 60 per cent is to be allowed on materials used in the manufacture of various tools when at least fifty per cent of the production cost has been incurred in Canada.
A drawback of 50 per cent is given on materials used in the manufacture of engines for the equipment of aircraft. After July 1, 1930, no drawback shall be paid unless at least 40 per cent of the cost of producing the finished engine has been incurred in Canada.
The Department of National Revenue has difficulty in administering the present tariff item 531 covering cloth for bookbinding. This item is repealed; a drawback of 99 per cent is granted instead. This will give the bookbinders practically the same concession.

In summing up the statement presented today little need be said, because, sir, the figures, speaking for themselves, require no words to emphasize the sound position of the Dominion's balance sheet. A general tone of optimism exists throughout Canada. Nevertheless, may I be permitted a word of iriendly caution as to the future.
To-day we are widening the inhabited frontiers, penetrating and developing our great northern domains. Federal and provincial governments, transportation companies, commercial corporations and individuals share in the work. It is a national undertaking of importance, for it not only develops Canada in a material way, but in addition, gives a better balance to our geographical groupings of population. Should we not profit by experiences of the past and keep this expansion within proper economic bounds, so that at no time will undue strain be placed either on the resources of the governments or of the investors.

speechtext: When the house rose at six o'clock last night I was endeavouring to explain why, in my opinion, the resolution, in so far as creating a statutory grade for the protein contents of grain, is difficult of application. I realize that there are a great many difficulties in the way of putting this into effect at the present time, but I am very much in favour of further research work in connection with it. I suggested to the minister-and may I emphasize it again-the necessity for increasing the facilities at the bureau at Winnipeg and giving Dr. Birchard all the help that he requires to carry out this work. I believe if that bureau is properly equipped and manned it will be a great help to the farmers of the prairies. A farmer who considers that he has grain of a high protein content and high protein quality can send his sample to this bureau and receive a test, and find out just what its value is before he ships it from his farm. It seems to me that would simplify matters very considerably, and I would again request the minister to agree to have this resolution sent to the committee on agriculture and colonization. I believe that, if it . is referred to that committee and those who are interested are given an opportunity to present their views, we will get some information that will put this house in a better position than at present to determine just in what way to proceed. If the grain dealers, representatives of the pool, the millers and the farmer's organizations can come and present their views, I believe that committee will be in a position to make some concrete and constructive proposals to this house as to how the matter should be further dealt with.

speechtext:
I shall be only
too glad to ask the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Malcolm) to make a return of the number of cars of grain actually dried. I think such a return will clear the matter up, because in talking to the elevator men I have been' informed that up to the close of navigation there is no drying of grain, and that in a great many of the private terminal elevators the driers are practically never used, being put there simply as a bluff.
Now, in regard to moisture content in grain, it has been found by experiment that wheat which is slightly bleached is not
damaged in any particular for milling into flour. Wheat that is heavily bleached is changed, but it is not damaged to anything like the extent that our grading system penalizes it to-day. For instance, there are times when the crop is of high quality as a whole, but there is some heavily bleached or sprouted wheat. At those times it has been the practice of the millers in this country, and also in fhe United States, to buy those heavily bleached and sprouted wheats at a premium in order to blend them with a high protein, high viscosity wheat so as to mill out a flour which will make a better baking flour, without using other commercial improvements. These wheats, under our present system, are placed in the No. 4 wheat for grade. That is they are put in with wheat containing a large percentage of green kernel or heavily frosted wheat, and heavily frosted wheat or wheat containing a large number of green kernels is a very poor milling wheat. This sprouted wheat which is a good milling wheat and the heavily bleached wheat should be kept separate altogether from the No. 4 so that it can be used for the purposes that I spoke of.
Let me say a word with regard to the buyers of our wheat in the world market. The miller of grain in Liverpool, or the European miller, is in this position in buying wheat:	He has to mill to the same standard
at all times, and must keep to that standard constantly, otherwise he will lose his customers. Therefore when the different wheats from different parts of the world start to come to Europe, he analyses those wheats and finds out how much wheat of different kinds he needs in order to mill to the standard he has maintained for years. In one year he will need a Canadian grain of high protein and high viscosity to a much greater extent than in another year. If the wheat of the world is low in protein and low in baking strength, that year he will need Canadian grain to a greater extent than another. He is willing to pay a premium for it, and would be only too willing to have our grain grade based upon the strength and the amount of protein that is in our wheat. The Canadian miller of grain is in a different position. He buys his grain in a country where we have ordinarily a large amount of high protein and high viscosity or high baking-strength wheat. Nevertheless this year the Canadian millers are buying thousands of cars of wheat, on the ordinary grade in the market, and in some cases are turning back into the trade as much as two-thirds of the cars that they have bought after
528	COMMON'S
Grading of Wheat-Mr. Ross (Moose Jaw)
having tested them in their laboratories. The protein of the Canadian crop this year is a bit lower than usual. In other words the Canadian miller this year is picking from the run of our crop the high protein wheat, and is turning back the lower protein wheats into the export channel. Or to put it another way, the poorer part of the Canadian wheat crop is going to the world's markets to set the price for the whole wheat crop of Canada.
In the United States the miller is in a different position still. In that country the greater part of the crop is of soft wheat, low protein, low baking-strength wheat. He is in a restricted market, and he is much more ready to bid high prices for high protein than anyone else, because he has to get that high protein to blend with his soft wheats in order to bring up the baking strength of his flour. Therefore, the examples that have been given in this house regarding the prices that will be paid for protein in the United States do not hold good as to Canadian grain or grain going to the world's markets, because the demands in the world's markets are not as great as they are in the restricted markets in the United States, or do not exist to such a great extent. In the Canadian market there is a very limited demand for high protein because our average crop is high protein content. In some years there is a demand in Canada for low protein wheat or soft wheat, bleached or sprouted wheat, to blend with the high protein wheat.
Now in regard to mixing. Our present Grain Act allows the buyers of grain in this country to mix grades. If you buy No. 3 northern grain there is a wide spread in that grade. A good No. 3 is just too poor to be a No. 2; a poor No. 3 is just too good to be a No. 4; a good No. 4 wheat is just too poor to be a No. 3; and a poor No. 4 is just too good to be a No. 5. Now the buyer of grain in this country to-day can buy a good car of No. 3 northern and a good car of No. 4 wheat, can mix the two together, and come out under our grade system with two cars of No. 3 northern at an advance this year of 12 to 13 cents per bushel. As a matter of fact there have been cars of grain this year of No. 3 northern straight grade, and the specially good No. 5 wheat could have been mixed and graded to make a straight 3 northern. I do not say that without assurance for this reason: this very crop year I picked from cars that were going through a specially good sample of 5 wheat, and I took an average sample of No. 3 northern, and mixed the two together in the proportion of fifty-fifty. I put the re-
suit of that mixing in front of an inspector under the board of grain commissioners, paid by the Dominion government, and it was graded by him as No. 3 northern wheat. However, I was not satisfied with that. I took it to another inspector, and had him grade it, and he got the same result. There was a difference in that case of 26 cents per bushel on the one carload of grain. A grading system that will allow things of this kind most assuredly should be changed. Such a thing as that is entirely wrong, and the people of western Canada who are growing grain today are losing millions of dollars as a result of our grading system.

I would also suggest to the Minister of Trade and Commerce that he call into conference with him the board of grain commissioners and tell them that we in this house are vitally interested in this being done and that they should facilitate in every way possible the elucidation of these matters. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Qu'Appelle (Mr. Millar), in bringing forward this resolution has done a very good service for the people of Canada. At the present time many people throughout the western part of this country are vitally interested in the grading of wheat. The selling of the wheat crop is often the one great venture of the year for the wheat farmer and during the present year there has been widespread dissatisfaction over the grades which are being given. It seems that the board of standards issues certain instructions each year, but often their instructions do not apply to all parts of the country. Their instructions may deal largely with rust conditions and things of that kind, and in certain parts of Canada the inspectors are given very little guidance and have only their own judgment to rely upon in grading the grain, a matter which is so vital to the producers. The present method, of course, is an arbitrary one, depending upon the individual judgment of the inspector, and many examples could be quoted where one inspector will assign a certain grade to a certain sample while another inspector will give the same sample an entirely different grade. Many things enter into their judgment in these cases, for instance, the colour of the grain, the number of unmatured kernels, the amount of starch in the sample and whether the grain has been slightly frosted or not.
In the wheat-growing provinces there are many varieties of grain. The older varieties are still used and still make up the standards, but many new varieties are being tried out by individual farmers. I realize that the department is doing a good deal to discourage farmers from planting these new varieties until they have been thoroughly tested out in the different experimental farms, but I know much grain does not comply with the older standards because these new varieties are being used. The chief inspector, I believe, says that there are about seventeen hundred different grades of grain at the present time. In a way we in Canada are in an especially good position as regards our grading 56103-34
system. I refer to the markets of Europe. While grain from the chief countries which compete with Canada is liable to be re-graded in Europe, European buyers will accept Canadian grades and this possibly would make it a little difficult to change our system of grading. Such countries as Australia, India and the Argentine are liable to have their grades changed or their grain re-graded in Europe, whereas Canadian grades are accepted.
As I have said, however, widespread dissatisfaction and a great deal of doubt exist in the minds of Canadian farmers as to whether they are really getting all they are entitled to get in selling their grain crop. Whether fairly or unfairly they often assume that they are not getting what is coming to them as producers of grain. For instance, when nearly all the grain of a district grades No. 4, they wonder whether all the flour produced from that grain will be No. 4 or not, and they also wonder if there is any way whereby buyers of grain could have their records checked up in order that it might be seen whether they sell the same quantity of, say grade No. 4, as they buy. If anyone doubts there is much dissatisfaction, he has only to consider what has been said by hon. members who have spoken on this subject, and if he does I am sure he will agree that an investigation is required into the present system of grading with the hope of finding some system that has more scientific accuracy in it.
The official standards for wheat do not at present contain any reference to protein content and they contain no element that constitutes a reliable indication of the protein content. We know that gluten, or the protein content, is the quality required chiefly by the bakers. We know that millers pay and are willing to pay a premium for high protein wheats, and we are not convinced that under present conditions this premium which they are willing to pay is fully reflected back to the wheat growers. This operates to the dissatisfaction of the producers of some of our choicest wheats. I refer to our dry land farmers. They are distant from milling centres and terminal markets and they' are largely at the mercy of the people who buy their grain. Surely, if a premium is being paid at all, it should be fully reflected back to the primary producer of the grain who worked so hard to bring his crop to the market.
I wish to read just a short extract from the Wheat Studies of the food research institute of Stamford university. It discusses the various



Grading of Wheat-Mr.. Coote
grades of grain and the methods of judging that grain, and it says:
Nevertheless, all things considered, the amount of gluten, that is, of protein, seems in the light of the present-day knowledge to be the nearest approach to an ideal index of baking strength available. The baker who depends upon it alone will now and then be deceived. If, however, he knows the variety and place of origin, of the wheat from which the flour is milled, he will less often be misled.
I contend, Mr. Speaker, that this is a subject which requires a good deal of investigation and very careful study. I am most firmly convinced, however, that the farmers of Canada are not satisfied with the present method of grading, and they hope that some better method may be worked out. The people in the United States are also alive to this condition, and the chairman of the United States board of review stated in conversation that:
If Canada should establish protein as a grading factor, the United States would be forced to do the same. Pressure was being brought to bear all the time. The United States laboratories at Washington were working hard on this question at the present time. He believed the bakers were driving the mills to furnish high protein flour, and competition between the mil's forced them to comply.
I believe that the wheat of Canada might have a better place on the markets of the world owing to its high protein content, and I think the farmers of Canada would be much happier if they did not have the impression that the present system was working unfairly to them.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think the hon. member for Qu'Appelle (Mr. Millar) is to be congratulated upon his persistence in keeping this subject before the House of Commons. It is a subject of great importance to the farmers of western Canada, and therefore of great importance to the country as a whole.
It is almost a waste of words to say that there is great dissatisfaction existing among the producers of grain in western Canada over our present grading system. Very much has been said in praise of our grading system, and possibly a good deal of it deservedly said. I think that a great deal of the dissatisfaction which undoubtedly exists has been caused by the lack of uniformity in our grading. It is very difficult under the present grading system as outlined in the Canada Grain Act to secure the uniformity which we ought to have. The chief inspector is reported to have made the statement when he was before a farmers' convention recently that grading was after all a matter of opinion. To producers the grading

of their wheat is too important a matter to be done simply upon the opinion of the inspector.
I do not know enough about the subject to say whether we would improve conditions by basing our grading system on the protein content of the wheat. Two years ago I visited the Minneapolis sample market while on my way to Ottawa and spent two days there, and while I was on the trading floor of their sample market I saw a buyer for one of the mills offer a premium of twenty-eight cents a bushel for one car of wheat over what he would offer for another car, although both were graded the same, No. 1 dark northern spring. The broker who was selling these two cars of wheat had secured a protein test of each car. One car tested something over fifteen per cent protein, and the other about ten and one-half per cent protein, and the difference in the protein content of those two cars of wheat made a difference in value, in the judgment of this buyer, of twenty-eight cents a bushel. There was also one instance in that season wheTe a premium of fifty-two cents was said to have been paid on the Minneapolis market for high protein wheat.
As the hon. member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Ross) said, it is generally believed that Canadian wheat is almost uniformly high in protein content, but we are probably assuming too much, with our present knowledge, if we assume that to be a fact. I personally would like to see this subject very carefully investigated. What I saw in Minneapolis convinced me that we diould at least make a thorough study of this subject, and I would suggest that this resolution be sent to the agriculture committee for consideration. I know that there will be much opposition raised to the suggestion that we should change our present system and base the grading of wheat upon its protein content, but I would point out that the sections of the present Grain Act covering the grading definitions take into consideration the milling value of wheat, and the milling value is, I think, largely determined, especially in the case of our higher grades, by the protein content. I do not know whether it is a fact that the protein content is the determining factor only in our higher grades of wheat. I think that sometimes our low grade wheat although it might show a high protein content, is not of very high milling value because the quality of the protein has been injured by weather ' conditions, by frost, possibly, or some other condition.
I do not think I should discuss our present grading system at very great length upon this resolution. I think it is sufficient to say

Grading of Wheat-Mr. Donnelly
that at least fifty per cent and possibly more, of our grain producers think that the system could be improved upon, and if that is a fact -we do not need to discuss the present system at any length at this time. I think we have sufficient justification for asking that this resolution be sent to the agricultural committee for consideration, and possibly we may get a recommendation from that committee as to any change they deem desirable in the act, or whether they think the subject should be further considered by our research department.

records show that in some of the laboratories many samples tested between 16 and 17 per cent, and maybe an odd one over that; but in my opinion, which I have arrived at as a result of conversation with grain men and millers, I believe anything in the neighbour-.hood of 13 or 14 per cent may be considered a high protein, and there is a great deal of wheat in the United States, and possibly some in western Canada, that will test less than 10 per cent. I believe the millers want a wheat for milling that will give a uniform baking value1. To secure that they want a uniform protein content, I do not know exactly what that protein content has to be, but I know that if they buy a quantity of wheat with too low a protein content, they will offer a premium for a car with an exceptionally high protein test, to mix with it and that is what has caused a high premium to be paid on the' market at Minneapolis for wheat with a high protein content. Whether that condition would obtain in Canada is hard to say, because many people here contend that so much of our wheat is of high protein content that there would not be sufficient demand to ensure the payment of very much premium for high protein wheat. However, I think we have evidence enough before us to warrant us in asking that this matter be referred for consideration to the committee on agriculture. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, with the others who have spoken I wish to congratulate the hon. member for Qu'Appelle (Mr. Millar) on having brought this resolution to the attention of the house. I consider this an important resolution to any farmeT in western Canada or to any man interested in farming, as it has to do with an honest endeavour on the part of the mover to secure for the farmer the right to demand and obtain the true value of his wheat. Now, we all concede that Canada is and will be for some time to come a distinctly agricultural country. The prosperity of the country depends upon agriculture. If the farmer is prosperous the whole country is prosperous and if western Canada has a good crop it stimulates trade throughout the whole Dominion, and that means a period of prosperity. Agriculture is and will be' for many years the

Grading of Wheat-Mr. Donnelly
basic industry of Canada. Any legislation therefore which enables the farmer to receive the true value of his product is good legislation and merits the support of the members of the house.
There are only two ways in which we can improve the conditions of the farmer and give him a greater net return for his product. One is by decreasing the cost of his production and the other is by increasing the price of wheat to the wheat grower. To increase the price to the wheat grower only two ways are open. One is to decrease the cost of the distribution of wheat. This problem has, to a great extent, been solved by the wheat pools in western Canada. It has been calculated that the wheat pools, by their work of distribution, have increased the price of wheat to the wheat grower by at least 25 cents a bushel, without in any way increasing the price of bread to the consumer. This has been brought about through the more efficient method of distribution, and we hope to see the wheat pools become still more efficient in the years to come. We can also increase the price to the wheat grower by inducing him to produce a better and higher grade of wheat. The wheat in western Canada is valued in the world's market chiefly on account of its hardness or the amount of protein which it contains.
Much work has been done in past years, and we hope to see much improvement in the years to come. This resolution asks that in fixing and applying standards of value account be taken of the basic property of wheat. That is the protein. Protein is that property of wheat which supplies viscosity to the dough: in other words, it is that property in the flour which, when made into dough and fermentation begins to take place, keeps and maintains each air particle separate and distinct from the other, as the dough will stretch and will not allow the air spaces to break into the other and so cause the dough to fall. Our system of grading has been in force for some years and is probably the best system in the world from a commercial standpoint. The system is convenient for commercial purposes and enables the wheat to be handled easily. It does not take into account the amount of protein contained in the wheat. In our grading system we only take into account the amount of moisture, the weight, the colour of the wheat, as well as the frost and so on, but we do not take into account the amount of protein. No account is taken whatever of the chief element for which the wheat is valued, and that is its protein. Our spring wheat grown in Canada is valued to-day throughout the

world for its protein content, and yet in our grading system no account whatever is taken of this, and though our system of inspection of wheat is old and has not been changed for years, and though we have had a commission for many years past looking into the grading of wheat, we have had no report whatever on inspection or grading of wheat, and I may say to-day that this year, above all years, there has been more complaint concerning the grading of our wheat than ever before. I believe the time has come when this government should look into the whole system of the grading and inspection of wheat.
If there is one fault I have to find with the resolution, it is that it does not go far enough. We should ask for a complete investigation into the whole system of grading and inspection of our wheat as it exists today. At the present time we have wheat grown in some parts of western Canada containing as low as seven or eight per cent of protein. It may have a bright, large and starchy kernel, but is low in protein, and on the other hand we may have wheat containing as high as 16 or 17 per cent protein, clear in colour, but small kernels, and yet these two grades of wheat, one containing B per cent and the other 17 per cent, receive exactly the same price on the world's market. This probably affects my constituency more than any other part of western Canada. I have the honour to represent a constituency in which there is a new soil, practically all virgin, lying in an area that does not receive too much moisture but just sufficient to raise a good, hard, red spring wheat. Yet, although we grow a wheat with a high protein content, we receive no more for it than do those who grow a product of lesser protein content, probably only seven or eight per cent. We are glad to note that during the past year the Saskatchewan Co-operative Wheat Producers Limited have been investigating the whole matter of the grading and inspection of grain as it exists in Canada to-day, with a view to securing such information as will enable them to recommend a more equitable application of the grading system to the individual farmer. It is also gratifying to know that the Dominion government, through the board of grain commissioners, have had scientists at work in this connection for some time, and we trust that the result of their efforts will be the acquisition of information of a practical nature. We are convinced that better results would be achieved if the services of more scientists could be secured in this field.

Grading oj Wheat*-Mr. Donnelly
I wish particularly to call the attention of the government to a portion of the report of the committee which was appointed by Saskatchewan Wheat Producers Limited, in which special reference is made to some of the faults which they discovered in the grading system. Let me quote one of their recommendations:
We next looked into the practice of grading as it is carried on at Winnipeg, checking the work of the samplers, deputy inspectors and chief inspector, and received much valuable information which has been submitted to you in detail. From Winnipeg we went to the head of the lakes and while there formed an opinion, which we still hold,, that there is a difference between the standard grade at Winnipeg and at the lake head. There has been some fairly severe criticism with regard to this opinion being expressed by members of the board, but notwithstanding anything that has been said, we are still of this opinion and would recommend that the resolution which was unanimously agreed upon by the inter-provincial meeting held in Calgary in March last be again taken up with the dominion government at the next session of parliament, the resolution being as follows:
"That steps be taken to provide that, in accordance with the Canada Grain Act, terminal elevators, both public and private, shall be compelled to maintain outturn grades of the same standard as that in use at primary inspection points; and further, that if the Canada Grain Act as at present constituted does not provide for this, steps be taken to obtain an amendment thereto to bring it into effect."
In this the claim is made that we have two standards of grain, one for inspection at Winnipeg and the other for inspection at Fort William. The grain commissioners also, at the same time, fix a standard whereby grain is sold at Fort William or at the head of the lakes, and as you will see from this recommendation it is felt that the standard applicable to wheat as sold at Fort William is not as high as the standard by which the wheat is bought at Winnipeg. This militates against the farmer, to the benefit of the distributor or the grain dealer. They claim that there is one standard by which they buy and an inferior or lower standard by which they sell. To substantiate this argument or to prove that the wheat, when it is being sold or is leaving the country, is not of as high a grade as when it is bought, let me refer the house to some of the work that has been done along this line. Forty-seven samples of wheat of contract grades were taken from Buffalo. These were inspected by both the government inspector at Winnipeg and the inspector attached to the Saskatchewan Wheat Producers Limited. From four to six samples were sent at a time from Regina to the inspector at Winnipeg out of these forty-seven
samples. Sixteen samples maintained their grade, and it was agreed by the inspector of the wheat producers as well as by the inspectors at Winnipeg that these were correct. Thirty-one were lowered by the government inspector, while twenty-one were lowered by the superintendent of the wheat producers. Every one of these samples had a small percentage of foreign grains such as barley, rye and so forth. Samples were also obtained from points on the Atlantic seaboard. From the public elevators at Baltimore, Philadelphia, Portland, Maine, New York and Montreal, samples of contract grades were taken and only one of these samples held the grade. That was sample No. 4 taken from the public elevator at Montreal. These samples were graded by Mr. Steele, of the Wheat Producers Limited, who was fully qualified to judge of the proper grade of wheat. Not satisfied with this, the Wheat Producers Limited had a number of samples, originally shipped across the Atlantic, brought back from England, and many of them I saw. There were from fifty to sixty of these samples. Invariably they were one grade lower, at least, than the contract grades at Winnipeg. The Wheat Producers Limited of Saskatchewan have had at least from forty to fifty samples of their shipments brought back from the old country. The general opinion seemed to be that our grades were more uniform, and if anything a little better than they were last year. Last year the old country millers complained bitterly about our No. 3 grade on account of its having dried wheat in it. This was almost a universal complaint, for it came not only from millers overseas but even from eastern Canadian millers. Nos. 1 and 2 grades were fairly uniform but they were just line grades; in other words, they were on the line between 1 and 2 or between 2 and 3, and invariably they were graded into the higher grade. This is some of the work that has been done and it shows that the grades that are shipped out of the country are lower than the grades received by the farmers at Winnipeg. This condition of affairs necessarily enables the private terminal elevators at the head of the lakes to indulge in the habit of mixing grain for export from Fort William and therefore lowering the standard of our wheat on the world's market.
Let me quo^e an example of mixing. I could cite many examples, but I will content myself with giving one to show the extent to which wheat is mixed at the head of the lakes, thereby reducing the standard. A fair example of the way wheat is mixed at Fort

This mixture was shipped out and sold on the markets of the world as No. 3 wheat. This is one of the worst examples of mixing that we have had and a great profit is made by this process at Fort William; and while our pool elevators are returning to the farmer in a great measure much of the profits of mixing, by indulging in the mixing process themselves, it is felt that it is an evil practice and it would be far better if it could be done away with entirely.
For the past ten years our standards of wheat have been depreciating in the markets of the world through this process of mixing, and though we are endeavouring by every means to increase the standards of all other farm products, it is regrettable that our major farm product should be allowed to suffer in this way. We try to raise the standard of our butter, our cheese, our bacon, our fruit, in fact the standard of every farm product but our major farm product-wheat, which to-day is being depreciated in the markets of the world. In this connection I find in the Regina Leader of January 17, 1928, the following article:
Canada is losing her world markets through failure to maintain her products at high quality, Mrs. IT. M. Aitkens of the institute branch, Ontario Department of Agriculture, declared to-day in addressing the Ottawa branch of the National Council of Women.
Discussing her impressions of Canada standing in the various countries of Europe which she recently visited, and in substantiation of her statement that Canadian produce was losing its former high ranking, Mrs. Aitkens said, "Canadian wheat is deteriorating; last year alone growers of the Dominion having lost $9,000,000."
This is a quotation from the report of the committee appointed by the board of directors of the Saskatchewan Co-operative Wheat Producers Limited.
In connection with this worlj we had found out from our general sales manager, Mr. D. L. Smith, and from the perusal of correspondence and cables received from the United Kingdom and continental Europe, that there was some dissatisfaction in connection with the standard of Canadian grain which was reaching those countries, a complaint being particularly strong 
in connection with our No. 3 Northern wheat. We also found a fairly general opinion expressed by terminal operators of long standing and by grain men generally that our grain standards were being gradually reduced, due partly to the many varieties of wheat that are being grown in the three provinces at this time, and due to the fact that most of the terminal elevators at the head of the lakes were being operated as private terminal elevators or mixing houses, and that very few of the terminaf elevators were operating under a public' terminal license, in fact only six of all the elevators in Fort William and Port Arthur at this time are operating as public terminal elevators.
The Department of Trade and Commerce should look carefully into this whole matter and endeavour by every means in its power to keep the standard of our wheat at the highest possible point in, the markets of the world. It is felt that there is no necessity for two standards, one at Fort William, the other at Winnipeg. We believe that we should have only one inspection point for wheat, and that it should be at Winnipeg. I am speaking, of course, entirely of wheat shipped out through Winnipeg and Fort William. I submit that there should be no inspection point at all at Fort William, and that the wheat which the farmer has to sell should be inspected at Winnipeg, and that the wheat which is sold for export from all private elevators should also be inspected at Winnipeg, even if the mixing system is allowed to continue. A sample of the wheat that is being prepared for export should be taken out of the private elevators and sent back tc Winnipeg, to be there inspected by the * same inspectors that inspected the farmer's wheat. We do not believe that the graders at Fort William are crooked, we do not believe that they are not d'oing their work efficiently, yet there exists in the public mind a feeling that these men are not doing their work as it should be done, that there is too much room for graft. When we take into account the spread in wheat to-day between 2 and 3 northern has been on an average throughout the whole season at least 15 cents, and that boatloads are being shipped of two, three and four hundred thousand bushels, we find that a difference in those grades involves a loss running from $30,000 to $60,000. Now when * it is borne in mind that the men who are doing this grading are only getting $2,500 to $3,000 a year-well, we cannot help but think the same sometimes as the man in the country, " human nature is human nature." In short, the chance for graft is too great. This chance should not be present. We think in fairness to the men themselves they should be. relieved of all suspicion and the government should take eveTy precaution to

Grading of Wheat-Mr. Bothwell
this end. In order to relieve the men of all suspicion of questionable methods, either in grading or taking samples, I believe it would be wise if the samples were not only taken at Fort William when the boat is being loaded, but again at Buffalo or at any other point where the boat is unloaded, these samples to be sent back to Winnipeg to confirm the former grades.
Let me say in conclusion, Mr. Speaker, that I heartily support this resolution, but I think it should be enlarged so as to take in the whole question of grading and inspection of wheat, and that it should be referred to the agriculture committee, to thoroughly investigate and report thereon.

subtopic: GRADING OF WHEAT
subsubtopic: PROPOSED REVISION OF STATUTORY DEFINITIONS OF GRADES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have listened to the discussion of this resolution with a great deal of interest. Every member from the prairie provinces must realize that the grading of wheat is a most important part of the great industry that is carried on in the west. Every year we hear complaints about the grading of wheat, and this past year has been no exception, in fact last fall I think there have been more complaints of wheat grading than ever before.
I am doubtful, though, if we are yet at the stage where we can accept this resolution. It reads:
That in the opinion of this house the statutory definitions applying to all contract grades of wheat in the western inspection division should be amended in such a manner as to provide for including protein as a factor.
I take it this means that if the house passes the resolution, immediately the duties imposed upon the Board of Grain Commissioners, through instructions from the Department of Trade and Commerce, to prepare an amendment to the Grain Act, but from what I have heard in this debate I am very doubtful whether we are yet ready to accept such an amendment. Yesterday in introducing the resolution the hon. member for Qu'Appelle (Mr. Millar), at page 497 of Hansard, quoted the following paragraph from the proceedings of the Research Council of Canada:
All endeavour so far has failed to disclose any method by which strength may be measured other than the baking test but this method is unsatisfactory for many reasons. It is inexact, depends chiefly on the skill of the operator, is time-robbing, and when completed it is impossible to express the results numerically or in a way that would be universally understood. Also reliance can scarcely be placed on a single test, and often as many as three bakings must be made to make certain of the results.
If that is a true statement of fact so far as the research council is concerned, surely we
are not yet ready to amend the act and make provision for taking the protein content as a factor in the grading of wheat, with all that that implies. I do not know just what effect it might have on the wheat industry in western Canada. And I should like to know what effect it might have on the mills at or near the points of inspection. These mills often purchase the wheat immediately it comes into Winnipeg, and we do not know just how long that grain is going to be held up in order to have these tests made. We do not know further what effect it may have upon the railway traffic in connection with moving the tremendous crop of wheat that we have in the west each year.
For these reasons, and also the fact that apparently the investigators are not yet able to give a definite report as to how protein content can be accurately obtained, also that they are not yet able definitely to fix what percentage or quality of protein should be taken to determine the value of wheat- as shown by a clipping from the Southwestern Miller, which I should like to read-I do not think we are yet ready for the change suggested in this resolution. The article to which I refer is dated at Kansas City, July 21, and reads as follows:
"The percentage and quality of protein is having more and more effect on the market price of wheat," says H. M. Bainer, director of the Southwestern Wheat Improvement Association. Continuing he says, "Millers and grain dealers are paying a good liberal premium for hign protein wheat, especially when they know that the protein is of good quality. The wide margin in price often paid at the same market on the same day for different lots of wheat of the same grade is almost always due to the difference in protein.
The country grain buyer cannot determine the protein content in wheat; the work is too intricate and special chemical equipment is necessary. The only way the wheat grower or grain buyer can determine the percentage of protein is by sending a small composite sample to the state grain laboratory or to a cereal chemist for analysis. Protein may run as low as 8 per cent and as high as 18 per cent, but 12 per cent is a good, high average."
I think it was the hon. member for South Oxford (Mr. Cayley) who inquired as to the protein content of our Canadian wheat. Taking the report of the Regina Leader last year as to the six more commonly tested wheats from the western station in the prairie provinces the results are as follows:

speechtext:
I desire to make just a few
observations before the amendment is put. I feel that the thanks of the house are due to the hon. member for Qu'Appelle (Mr. Millar), and those associated with him, for the persistency with which they have kept this important question before the house and the country generally. For the last forty years, at least every time there has been an off-year in the matter of grades, there has been an agitation and a natural and proper demand for some betterment in the matter of our wheat grading system. The fact that not much improvement has been made is not an argument in 
favour of giving up the fight, but rather an argument in favour of pressing onward until that betterment has been obtained in every possible respect. The house will recall, at least those members who have had the opportunity of reading Dean Eutherford's account of his visit to the old country will do so, that when the dean visited the old land he could find no miller or importer who would venture the opinion that wheat could be successfully graded on a protein basis for export, because of the great difficulty of retaining the identity of the various wheats on that basis. I will not enter into a discussion of the matter, except to point out that we have a tremendous multiplicity of grades now, and anything that will tend to increase the present number, without bringing about a commensurate advantage, should be avoided. Take for instance No. 1 northern. It may be tough or damp; it may be rejected for smut, and I do not know what else. If we had to grade it on the basis of the protein content-whether it were 16 per cent, or 15 per cent, or 14 per cent, or some other percentage-that would multiply the number of grades very considerably. While that is the case, something I think can be done and the hon. member for Macleod (Mr. Coote) indicated it. The prices are governed, at least for the home market and in the United States, very substantially on the basis of protein. Where the millers are right on the ground and can see the sample they are buying on the sample market, and there is very little damage, if any at all, from frost, they can reasonably well buy on that basis. But on the other hand, where this low grade wheat is due to either frost or rust, grading on a basis of protein content might be quite misleading and might, as a matter of fact, have the very opposite effect to that which is contemplated. As I have already pointed out, the very lowest grade wheat, namely, No. 6, might run just as high in protein content as the highest grade, namely, No. 1. The protein content in the case of wheat will mean nothing unless the quality goes with it, and everybody knows the quality cannot go with a No. 6 northern wheat which has been put into that grade as a result of damage by frost; neither can it go with wheat affected by rust, because the yield will be so adversely affected. The whole question, therefore, is properly a matter for the committee on agriculture to consider, and it Should also be the subject of research.
I hope the house will not draw any wrong inferences from the suggestion of the hon. member for Macleod (Mr. Coote) that there is a possible difference of twenty-eight cents

Grading oj Wheat-Mr. Vallance
a bushel with regard to two samples of wheat because of the difference in the protein content,
If the quality of the wheat were adversely affected in any of the ways in which Canadian wheat may suffer damage, a greater quantity of protein in content would have no appreciable effect in counteracting that * damage; as a matter of fact the effect might be the opposite to what is contemplated. If we refer this matter to the committee on agriculture we shall have the decided advantage of being able to call in our experts, for instance, Doctor Shutt, Dominion chemist, who has done a great deal of experimenting in this respect, and Mr. Newman, Dominion cerealist. We could also call in Mr. Harcourt, of Guelph, who is in charge of one of the best milling and baking laboratories in Canada, if not in America, and we could find out from them first-hand just to what extent the protein content can be made use of without our being misled in the direction indicated by various speakers.
I should like to make a few observations with respect to the remarks made by the hon. member for Willow Bunch (Mr. Donnelly) on another matter which is correlated to this one, and that is with respect to the standards of our outgoing grain from the head of the lakes. The evidence he produces goes to show that a large number of samples of outgoing grain differed very materially from the samples where the standards were set at the time of purchase, namely, in Winnipeg. Without doubt that is a very important point, and I wish to draw the attention of the house to the fact that provision was made in the Turgeon report for correcting just that sort of thing, but at that time the committee on agriculture and the house were not prepared to move in the direction of the Turgeon report. I have no doubt whatever if the request were made by the growers through their pools that grain which is mixed at the public terminals at Fort William should be graded on the same basis as the grain at Winnipeg, there would be a disposition on the part of the agriculture committee of the day and this house to accept such a suggestion coming from such a source.
Some hon. members from the west who can recall the late eighties of last century know that mixing grew to such enormous proportions during the latter part of that decade that the grain trade itself came to parliament and asked to be saved from its own conduct. In the year 1900 the new Grain Act was introduced as a result of the agitation of that time and mixing was prohibited. About 1912 -and I need not go back to the reasons for this-mixing was resorted to again, and it
has been going on and on, and being more generally practised, until we now have the complaints referred to by the hon. member for Willow Bunch. In my estimation we shall have history repeating itself. This evil will cure itself because those who are practising it and the farmers themselves will, in due course come to parliament and ask that this condition be remedied. I am very much in favour of the amendment and all the facilities of my department will be made use of for the purpose of having the parties to whom I have referred brought before the committee to give evidence.

Mr. Speaker, I am rising to second this amendment because I believe the proper place to discuss this resolution and to do it justice is in the committee cm agriculture. As has been pointed out by the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Motherwell), there we can have the millers, growers and others who are interested come before that committee to give their views on this matter. Perhaps this resolution and the amendment are somewhat premature, because I think the whole proposition would benefit if discussion of the matter were deferred until the report of the research council is available. We would then be in a better position to discuss the matter intelligently.
It is quite apparent in this debate that every member from the western provinces has attempted in some way to expose the evils of the present grading system, but I do not think all the evils have been printed out. The hon. member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Ross) pointed out one particular instance, namely, the moisture content of wheat. In a year such as the crop year 1927, where we had a large quantity of tough wheat, this was a very pressing question with the farmers of western Canada, and I had pointed out to me on more than one occasion that too much latitude seemed to be given within the grade, for instance, that wheat shall contain 14.4 per cent of moisture in order to get into dry wheat. It is common knowledge, at least to us western farmers, that the greater bulk of the wheat grown on the open prairies of Saskatchewan and Alberta contains as low as 11 per cent of moisture, and the farmer who is growing wheat with 11 per cent of moisture content feels that he is being somewhat penalized because he has to accept it as containing 14.4 per cent of moisture. Therefore, we are selling on the world market wheat of a grade that may contain 14.4 per cent of moisture although on many occasions we are growing wheat with a great deal less moisture content. As long as there is a latitude within

I believe, from my experience after growing wheat for twenty-two years on the western plains, that we, the farmers, sell our wheat at the maximum moisture content and that when it goes on to the world market it is sold at the maximum, thus giving the grain trade a great deal of latitude in the mixing. I wish to rise in support of the .amendment. I am of opinion that the proper thing to do in this regard is first to get the opinion of the national research institute, when that organization is set going, so that we can arrive at as definite a scientific opinion as is possible.
As I understand it, the aim of the resolution was to make the protein content if not the determining factor at least a greater factor than it is at present in determining the grade of wheat. I was much impressed by the remarks of the hon. member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Ross) when he pointed out that although protein is an important factor it is not always the only factor which the millers require in 'buying wheat. In the United States protein is very largely the determining factor for this reason: Minneapolis is a very large milling centre. It draws its wheat from a large area where the wheat is of low protein content. It is only on the northern borders of Montana and Dakota that wheat of high protein content is produced. Consequently the millers of Minneapolis, wishing to make a flour up to their standard grade, are looking for wheat of a high protein content to tone up the wheat which they get from other parts of the country that is of a lower protein content. Protein is therefore always at premium in the Minneapolis market. They have their grades over there just as we have here. You will find on the Montana side of the line that wheat of a certain grade, selling say for one dollar a bushel, will, if it contains a large percentage of protein, bring a premium of sometimes as high as twenty-eight cents a bushel. But that would not apply univer-

sally; it would not apply in this country. Our wheat is very largely of high protein content. Protein, then, not being so scarce in Canada as it is in the United States, would not necessarily command the same premium.
_ What is the practice at the present time in grading wheat in this country? We grade largely by the eye and by the scale. If the wheat weighs sixty pounds to the bushel and contains a certain percentage of bard, bright red, vitreous kernels, these can be inspected and judged by the eye, and that wheat is put into No. 1 grade. Much has been said of the dissatisfaction over the grading that has existed in the west during the past year. I have never seen so much dissatisfaction over our present grading system as I have this year, but is that dissatisfaction due to the presence or absence of protein? I do not think so. I think the trouble is this: The farmer looks at his sample and he sees that the great bulk of it is composed of hard, bright red, vitreous kernels, sand he thinks that that surely will grade No. 1. He ships his car, and a sample is taken at Winnipeg. The inspector looking at that wheat is not looking for hard, bright red, vitreous kernels; he is looking for defective kernels, and if he finds a certain number of green, frozen or damaged kernels, he puts that wheat down a grade.
It seems to me that possibly the Grain Act might be improved in this way, without waiting for such a reference as this: The inspection department will not separate wheat from wheat. If you ship a carload of wheat which contains a certain percentage of wild oats, it might go through as No. 1, but if you ship another car of identically the same wheat, but containing, instead of wild oats, a certain percentage of small, green, shrunken kernels, that wheat will be degraded because they will not separate wheat from wheat. Now these damaged kernels could be taken out just as easily as the wild oats.

There is another question, and that is how to get for the farmer the true value of his wheat. To-day the farmers with No. 1 wheat, whether it be good No. 1 or a poor No. 1, get the same price, but there might be a difference of from five to ten cents in the milling value as between two cars of No. 1 wheat; and the same would apply to the other grades. The remedy for that situation would be a sample market, with samples within the grade, if you will, where professional buyers representing the terminals in which this wheat would be mixed could attend, and where every carload would be tested. Mr. Speaker, the question of grading wheat according to its protein content was of more importance years ago, and in common with the hon. member for Lisgar (Mr. Brown) I am of the opinion that it is not even practicable for the farmer of western Canada to market wheat under that method. Some years ago we urged the government to establish a sample market. They did not do so, for obvious reasons. I would say that we should by all means establish a sample market, so that the farmer would get the intrinsic value of his wheat; but having to export about nine-tenths of this great wheat crop of Canada the difficulty is for any foreign miller to get the wheat he has bought on sample to its destination where he would be able to take advantage of it, and the protein content he has bought, at his own mill. It has to pass through so many terminals and transfer between Fort William and the seaboard that the identity of any wheat bought on sample is.bound to be submerged in the common whole. In the first place, it is sent forward to Fort William in such quantities that after it is graded according to its content of protein at Winnipeg, bills of lading are exchanged by all companies and it is unloaded at the terminal most convenient to be used at the time.

I believe that this principle of grading wheat is not as yet practicable. Besides, I think the need of the growler has been obviated somewhat by about 60 or 70 per cent of it now being marketed by himself through the pool method, and he is to-day getting nearer the value of his product than he ever did 'before. If it were profitable to transfer and to preserve the identity of the wheat between the grower and the ultimate miller, I would then be in favour of such a system; but at present I cannot see that it will help the grower very much. I am not against the resolution and shall be glad to have it discussed in committee, but at present I cannot see that it is at all practicable.

speechtext:
I explained the bill
briefly on the first reading and I hardly think it necessary to discuss it at any great length now. I will ask the house to pass the second reading and allow the bill to go to the committee on privileges and elections for detailed consideration. The object is to obviate the disfranchisement of clergymen, school teachers and students when, in the pursuit of their various callings or studies, they find it necessary to change their place of residence from one constituency to an- , other within the period during which, under the present law, such transfer of residence would disqualify them. This period covers about four months prior to the date of the election. Most of our federal elections are held in the fall of the year. Practically every federal election since 1896 has been held in the fall, and clergymen usually change their pastorates during the summer months, while school teachers take up new duties about the first of'September and university students and those in business colleges about the first of October. Should any of these three classes change their place of residence at the beginning of their respective terms they are disfranchised under the present act if the election happens to take place in the fall. The act provides that

Dominion Elections Act
the voter shall reside in his present polling subdivision for a period of sixty days prior to the issue of the writ of election, and as the writs are usually issued about two months before the election it means that the voter must reside in his division for about four months preceding the election.
The question may be asked, why make an exception in favour of clergymen, school teachers and students? I would point out that under the act as it stands a similar exception is made in favour of railway employees, sailors and commercial travellers, in the interests of whom advance polls are provided.
I brought down this bill last year and it received its first reading but it could not be dealt with at that session. I would remind the house that before introducing the bill then I took the matter up with Colonel Biggar, then chief electoral officer, and discussed it fully with him, and he agreed that the amendment proposed should be carried into the act. As I say, objection might be raised to confining it to these three classes.

All students entering these institutions are obliged to make application, wherein they must state their place of residence. The secretary, or whoever happens to have charge cf such matters, the registrar of the institution, perhaps, knows pretty well the history of every student coming in. Moreover, the bill provides that the person making application to
