The same thing applies to school teachers and clergymen:. When people apply for positions as school teachers the secretary of the school district, to whom the applications are sent, learns their history to a certain extent. The' secretary of every school district knows where a particular teacher comes from, how long he has been in his last place of residence, and gets sufficient information generally on which to enable the registrar to decide whether or not the applicant is qualified to vote. In the case of clergymen, I believe, every religious denomination has some board or other body that passes upon all transfers from one pastorate to another. In each of these three cases, therefore, the record can be checked up if necessary, and the onus is placed upon the applicant who, when he applies to the registrar to have his name included in the list, must furnish satisfactory proof that, apart from residence, he is qualified to vote. Mr. Speaker, I am not a member of the committee on privileges and elections and consequently will not have an opportunity of taking part in the discussion of this bill should it be referred to the committee. There is no analogy between the advanced poll provided for by the Dominion Elections Act and the purpose of this bill. The advanced poll only gives to the individual voter an opportunity to vote in the riding where he or she is entitled to vote; but this bill proposes to give the right to three particular classes in the community to vote in a constituency other than that in which under the act they now would be entitled to exercise their franchise. If the hon. member wants to shorten the time of qualification for voting, he should have brought in a bill aptly worded, and made all classes equal in this respect; but this bill applies to three particular classes, students, clergymen and teachers, and puts them in a preferred category. There are other men and women who may find themselves in exactly the same difficulty at election time as the people in question, and1 why should they be deprived of the privilege to be granted- by this amendment? Men engaged in railroad work and harvesters cannot vote at the advanced polls provided for under the act, although they have a right to the franchise. I am as anxious as the hon. member is to give every elector an opportunity to cast his vote at election time, but I am opposed to granting favours to a few and thus creating inequalities undei our electoral law. The hon. member has given the number of students, clergymen and teachers who would be benefited by the passage of this bill, but although he gives those figures on the authority of the Bureau of Statistics, it does not follow that all those people are entitled to vote; a large percentage of the students, for instance, may be under the age of twenty-one, and others may not be Canadian citizens. I have no objection to this bill going to the committee on privileges

and elections, but I do hope that that committee will thoroughly look into the inequalities to which I have drawn attention and put every section of the community on an equal basis.

speechtext:
Mr. J. C. BRADY (Skeena) moved the second reading of Bill No. 38, to amend the Bankruptcy Act,
He said: Mr. Speaker, under the Bankruptcy Act each province becomes a bankruptcy district, but the governor in council may divide such districts into two or more divisions and appoint an official receiver for each division. In the centre of British Columbia, an immense area through which are scattered many small towns and business centres, there are only two official receivers, one at Vernon and the other at Prince Rupert, and tremendous distances have to be travelled by the debtor in order to appear before the official receiver for examination. The purpose of the amendment is not to interfere with the basic principles of the act but simply one of procedure in examination of the debtor and to obviate the present necessity of the debtor being obliged to travel so far to the detriment of the creditors, because his travelling expenses naturally come out of the estate. This bill would make the Bankruptcy Act operative in those areas wherein to-day it is . inoperative, due to the conditions that I have just referred to. In other words, it would enable creditors there to benefit by the act as they do in urban centres.
Let me give the house an illustration typical of the difficulties in securing a debtor's examination in those areas. . A bankrupt who formerly carried on business near Prince George is now resident in Vancouver. From Vancouver to Prince George the distance by the Pacific Gre'at Eastern railway is 480 miles, and via Prince Rupert by w^ater and rail the distance is about 1,200 miles. Now, the debtor is obliged under severe penalties to travel to Vernon to appear for examination before the official receiver of the district

Bankruptcy Act
wherein he formerly resided. Later he must go to Prince George where the creditors' meeting would naturally take place. The purpose then of the amendment is not to interfere with the basic principles of the act but to render the act operative in those areas wherein to-day it is not possible for the creditors to benefit by it. I think, therefore, that anybody who has studied the bill and read the observations set forth therein will have no difficulty in seeing that it is of great importance that the creditors be enabled to get something at least out of the estate. In one particular instance where the act was taken advantage of the creditors were obliged to pay the debtor's expenses on two occasions and yet they received no benefit whatsoever out of the estate. The purpose, therefore, of the amendment is simply to render the act operative* throughout the whole of Canada, and likewise to enable the creditor or the creditors to receive the benefits which it was intended by the act that they should receive.

This bill having been printed only
a couple of days I admit that I have not been able to give the matter the consideration it deserves. The Bankruptcy Act was put into our statutes after long consideration by
committees of the house, and every section of it was carefully studied. I am rather reluctant, therefore, to change the act without giving the fullest consideration to the proposed change. However, I will say this to my hon. friend: I admit that the act as it is may in some special cases involve rather a hardship. Under section 128 of the act the debtor is required, within three days of the assignment, to present himself before the official receiver for examination, and that under penalty of imprisonment. I think the ordinary practice is to have this examination at the same time as the debtor presents his assignment to the official receiver. He has to travel some distance, a long distance in some cases, and at considerable expense. In some cases there are not many assets, and even if there are assets the debtor personally has no money. Even with a provision that he should be reimbursed out of the proceeds of the assets he could not go for the examination. On the other hand I am advised by the officers in charge of the administration of the law that they do not know of any case where a man has been imprisoned because he did not, owing to lack of funds, go for his examination. I may say to my hon. friend that those are obstacles, but they were purposely put into the act in 1923 because of the flood of assignments which occurred at that time, especially in rural districts. In my own province it was considered a plague, and those obstacles were placed in the way of these many assignments, which were regarded as a real danger.
Now the question is whether the time has come to remove the obstacles and in what way that shall be done. One method would be to appoint more official receivers. For instance in the province of Quebec there are at present thirteen official receivers and thirty judicial districts. If there were an official receiver in every district there would be thirty instead of thirteen. I am considering the advisability of authorizing the official receiver to appoint a deputy in some cases in other parts of the district. I may say to my hon. friend from Skeena (Mr. Brady) that as far as his province, and I think his district, is concerned, I have come to the conclusion that an official receiver should be appointed at Prince George. I think this would go a long way to remove the difficulties of which my hon. friend complains. The question of distributing the work between the judges of the high court and of county courts is also engaging the attention of the department. As to authorizing a notary public or minor magistrate to do the work which

10.000	cubit feet per second by way of the Chicago drainage canal to the Mississippi river.
2.	The joint report of the international waterways commission to the governments of the United States and Canada, dated May 3, 1906, recommending, amongst other things, that a diversion for sanitary purposes not exceeding
10.000	cubic feet per second be authorized for the Chicago drainage canal.

10.000	cubic feet per second for the Chicago drainage canal.
4.	All reports, correspondence or documents in the possession or under the control of any department of the government of Canada, which would tend to substantiate or to qualify the statement made to the foreign relations committee of the United States Senate, when the waterways treaty of 1909 was under consideration, that the representatives of the government of Canada "consented to leave out of this treaty any reference to the drainage canal, and we are now taking 10,000 cubic feet per second for the drainage canal which really comes out of this lake system."
5.	Copies of all correspondence, reports or documents relating to any protests made by or on behalf of the government of Canada against the diversion of waters from lake Michigan by the sanitary district of Chicago.
He said: The subject of the right of the Chicago sanitary district and of the state of Illinois to divert water at Chicago has been discussed in this house on a number of occasions, and the present Minister of the Interior (Mr. Stewart) made remarks in regard to the matter on March 26, 1924, again on June 3, 1924, and more recently in this house during the session of 1926. On January 25, 1926, tlie Minister of the Interior, in the course of a review of the whole matter, made to the house a formal statement in which he referred to a judgment of the Supreme Court of the United States dated January 5, 1925, restraining the Chicago sanitary district from withdrawing water from lake Michigan through the Chicago drainage canal in excess of the quantity then authorized by the United States Secretary for War. The Minister of the Interior then said:
This judgment-*
Referring to the judgment of the United States federal court.
-recognized for the first time, that the diversion affects and was contrary to Canadian rights under the Boundary Waters treaty of 1909.
I examined that judgment at some length, but I was unable to find in the terms of the judgment any such recognition as suggested by the Minister of the Interior. In any case the injunction was obviated by the fact that the United States Secretary for War, on March 3, 1925, granted a further permit to the Chicago sanitary district to withdraw water up to the quantity then required. The Minister of the Interior on that occasion also referred to a bill then before the United States Senate which "provides for the construction of a nine-foot navigable channel in the Illinois and Mississippi rivers based on the diversion froin lake Michigan through the sanitary district canal of an amount of water not to exceed 10,000 cubic feet per second." The minister continued:
The government is fully alive to the menace of the provisions of this bill to the navigation, power and other interests of the great lakes and St. Lawrence river, and is registering with the United States government a vigorous protest against its passage in so far as it contemplates the withdrawal of water from the great lakes.
It seems to me, Sir, most important in view of subsequent developments that these protests, such as they are, should be laid before the house so that the house may really understand the nature of the position taken by the government as represented by the minister.
On June 7, 1926, the United States Supreme Court referred three suits then pending in the federal courts-in which twelve states appeared as complainants against the state of Illinois and the Chicago sanitary district as defendants, all of which were consolidated and referred-to Charles Evans Hughes, as master, to take the evidence and to report thereon. The appointment of master in the federal courts of the United States, as it is in our own courts, is usually made of an appointee versed in the law, but of some impecunious lawyer who has not very much of a practice to occupy his attention. The appointment of a former secretary of state of the United States, a former governor of the state of New York, and an ex-judge of the supreme court of the United States, seems to suggest that the appointment of Mr. Hughes had political as well as judicial significance.
The prolonged inquiry before Mr. Hughes as special master, which continued from November 8, 1926, to June 23, 1927, was at length completed, and in November, or early in De-

546	COMMONS
Chicago Drainage Canal-Mr. Cahan
cember last, Mr. Hughes filed his report, which seems to be of special interest to this country. In this report Mr. Hughes briefly finds:
That the congress of the United States has power to regulate the Chicago diversion and to determine whether and to what extent it should be permitted;
That congress has by various enactments conferred authority upon the United States Secretary of War to regulate such diversion;
That the permit of the Secretary of War under which such diversion is now being made is valid and effective according to its terms;
That there is, in law and in fact no unlawful or illegal diversion of waters at Chicago.
In other words, in popular newspaper parlance, there is no "Chicago steal" so far as the United States is concerned. This report is satisfactory to this country, I should think, at least in this respect, in that if it is confirmed, as seems likely, it affirms unconditionally that, so far as the United States is concerned, the congress of the United States has exclusive control over this diversion at Chicago. So that so far as Canadian interests are affected thereby, it would seem that the federal government of the United States must accept full responsibility.
Healing with conclusions of fact, that report also affirms what has been the contention made in this house by members of the government, namely, that the effect of a diversion of 8,500 cubic feet per second has been to lower the mean levels of lakes Michigan and Huron six inches, the mean levels of lakes Ontario and Erie approximately five inches, the mean levels of the connecting rivers, bays and harbours, which have the same mean levels as the lakes I have mentioned, to the same extent respectively, and that each additional diversion of 1,500 cubic feet per second would lower the above levels by approximately one inch more; and finally there is the conclusion of fact from the evidence that if this diversion at Chicago were ended, assuming that other diversions remain the same, the mean levels of the lakes and rivers affected by the Chicago diversion would be raised in about five years in the case of lakes Michigan and Huron, and in about one year in the case of lakes Erie and Ontario, to the same levels as they previously were before they had been lowered respectively by the Chicago diversion.
So far the report was well within the bounds of the reference to Mr. Hughes, but in the evidence as submitted to him there were certain reports which had been made by the old international waterways commissionin which the American members and the Canadian

members of that commission had concurred, and which came under review by Mr. Hughes in making his report; and he perhaps goes beyond the scope of his reference, or, at least, the finding which he made in that respect is not binding upon Canada at all events. Mr. Hughes suggests that Canada has no valid ground of complaint under the waterways treaty of 1909, and that, in fact, Canada is now precluded by the conduct and consent of its representatives and by the terms of the waterways treaty of 1909 from making any effective protest against such diversion.
The evidence discloses the following sign,-ficant facts;
For many years prior to 1909, the congress of the United States had under consideration the diversion of 10.000 cubic feet of water per second from lake Michigan into the Illinois river and thence to the Mississippi river for the purposes of the sanitary district of Chicago, and also to provide a connection between the navigation of the great lakes and the Mississippi river and its tributaries.
I shall not review at length in the short time at my diposal the various statutes passed by the congress of the United States under which these diversions were authorized.

These early statutes to which Mr. Hughes refers in his report were passed by the congress of the United States, some ten years prior to the negotiation of the waterways treaty of 1909. On November 18, 1900, a board of engineers, appointed under the act of congress of March

Chicago Drainage Canal-Mr. Cahan
3, 1899, referred to the drainage canal as of ''sufficient depth and width for any possible requirements of navigation", and reported that "from the west end of this canal the waters of lake Michigan, in a steady flow amounting to from 5,000 to 10,000 cubic feet per second, are discharged into the bed of Des Plaines river and are carried thence down the Illinois river to the Mississippi".
Subsequently further permits were issued, and then we come to the appointment of the first international waterways commission. This commission was formed in pursuance of an act of congress of the United States, known as the River and Harbour Act, of June 13, 1902, and with the permission of the house I would like to place this one clause of that act on Hansard without reading it:
The president of the United States is hereby requested to invite the government of Great Britain to join in the formation of an international commission to be composed of three members from the United States and three who shall represent the interests of the Dominion of Canada whose duty it shall be to investigate and report upon the conditions and uses of the waters adjacent to the boundary lines between the United States and Canada including all of the waters of the lakes and rivers whose natural outlet is by the river St. Lawrence to the Atlantic ocean, also upon the maintenance and regulation of suitable levels and also upon the effect upon the shores of these waters and the structures thereon and upon the interests of navigation by reason of the diversion of these waters from or change in their natural flow and further to report upon the necessary measures to regulate such diversions and to make such recommendations for improvements and regulations as shall best subserve the interests of navigation in said waters.
It provided for a commission on which Canada should 'be represented by three Canadian members to be appointed by the government of Canada, the United States by three American members to be appointed by the government of the United States, who were to form an international commission. These six members were to represent the interests of their respective countries, and it was their duty to investigate and report upon the conditions and uses of the water adjacent to the boundary line between the United States and Canada, including all of the waters of the lakes and rivers whose natural outlet is by the river St. Lawrence into the Atlantic ocean; also upon the maintenance and regulations of suitable levels, and also upon the effect upon the shores of these waters and the structures thereon, and upon the interests of navigation, by reason of the diversion oif these waters from or change in their natural flow, and so on. The Canadian government, of which Sir Wilfrid Laurier was then Prime Minister, accepted' the invitation of the

The commission held its first meetings in Toronto on June 14 and 15, 1905. The United states Board of Engineers reported to congress on January 18, 1905, as follows:
The Chicago drainage canal was brought into use in January, 1900. It has not yet been completed to its full capacity as desired. When fully completed it will have a capacity of about
10,000	cubic feet per second flowing at a low velocity. As now constructed it has a depth of about 22 feet and a bottom width in different parts, 110 feet, 160 feet and 202 feet respectively. It constitutes a navigable channel, able to accommodate the largest vessels now navigating the great lakes. It extends from the Chicago river to Lockport, where it discharges into the Des Plaines river. . . In preparing its estimates the board-
That is the United States board-

The effect of this diversion upon the level of the great lakes was even then clearly apparent. In the same report, the United States board of engineers says:
The effect upon the level of lake Michigan of withdrawing 10,000 cubic feet per second for an indefinite period has been the subject of elaborate investigation under the office of the lake survey at Detroit, and the conclusion reached is that the final effect will be to lower the level about six inches.
Which was as subsequently found in the evidence adduced before Mr. Hughes last year. Their report continues:	1
The canal is not yet completed. It was designed to take up eventually a volume of 10,000 cubic feet per second. This represents about five per cent of the flow over Niagara falls which is about 222,400 cubic feet per second. The Chicago drainage canal when completed will, according to a calculation furnished by an engineer of the Canadian section of the commission, lower the level of lake Huron by six inches and the level of lake Erie by four and a half inches. Then on January 4, 1907, the following year, the Canadian members of the international waterways commission reviewed and again reaffirmed their recommendations of April 25, 1906, and also reaffirmed the joint recommendation of the international waterways commission of May 3, 1906, that:
A diversion for sanitary purposes, not to exceed 10.000 cubic second feet, be authorized for the Chicago drainage canal.
That recommendation was signed by the Canadian members, Messrs. George C. Gibbons, chairman, and W. F. King and Louis Coste, members, and Thomas Cote, secretary. They closed their report as follows:
The position at Niagara falls has been dealt with having regard to the exceptional circumstances there existing and taking into consideration the large permanent diversion by way of the Chicago drainage canal.
On January 4, 1907, tlje joint commission also reported to their respective governments. I have not time now to review at length that most extraordinary report, but I merely quote from the summary contained in the report as jointly prepared:
The diversion of 10,000 cubic feet of water per second at Chicago will render practicable a waterway to the Mississippi river fourteen feet deep.
This joint report, in which the Canadian members concurred, after reviewing all the facts, formally recommends:
Careful consideration of all the circumstances leads us to the conclusion that the diversion of
10,000	cubic feet per second through the Chicago river will, with proper treatment of the sewage from areas now sparsely occupied, provide for all the population which will ever be tributary to that river, and that the amount named will therefore suffice for the sanitary purposes of the city for all time. Incidentally, it will provide for the largest navigable waterway from Lake Michigan to the Mississippi river which has been considered by congress.
I wish to put on Hansard their joint recommendation in the form in which it appears:
We therefore recommend that the government of the United States prohibit the diversion of more than 10.000 cubic feet per second for the Chicago drainage canal, all of which is respectfully submitted.
W. F. King, chairman, Canadian Section.
Geo. C. Gibbons, Louis Coste, members, Canadian Section.
O. H. Ernst, Brig.-General U.S. Army, retired. Chairman, American Section.
Geo. Clinton, E. E. Haskel, members, American Section.
Attest: W. Edward Wilson, Secretary, American Section.
Thos. Cote, Secretary, Canadian Section.
On March 9, 1908, the Canadian members of the international waterways commission,
who were then George C. Gibbons, Louis Coste and William J. Stewart, made a supplementary report to the Canadian government reaffirming the recommendation of the joint commission of May 3, 1906, that:
A diversion for sanitary purposes, not to exceed 10,000 cubic feet per second, be authorized for the Chicago drainage canal.
Thereupon the government of Canada, with the full knowledge of the reports cited, began the negotiations with the government of the LTnited States that resulted in the waterways treaty of 1909, which was signed at Washington on January 11, 1909 and subsequently confirmed by this parliament. That treaty was negotiated, as nearly as I can ascertain from a study of the record, by three members of the Canadian government, Hon. Mr. Pugsley, since deceased, Mr. afterwards Sir George Gibbons, also deceased, and the then Minister of Justice, who is now a member of the upper house, Sir Allen Aylesworth. When the matter of the ratification of this treaty came before the house, Mr. Aylesworth, as he was then, said on December 6, 1910:
I take, with each of my colleagues, the fullest responsibility for recommending the acceptance of the treaty which is under consideration.
I quote from page 908 of Hansard of 191011. Sir Wilfrid Laurier, then Prime Minister, said:
I may say it was only after careful and exhaustive consideration on my part that 1 agreed to accept the treaty as it has been written.
The Hon. Elihu Root, who was then Secretary of State for the United States, and who negotiated the treaty on behalf of that country, in submitting the draft treaty to the foreign relations committee of the United States Senate, said.
I have carefully guarded the terms of this treaty in order not to include lake Michigan and not to involve Senator Cullom's constituents in the drainage canal in this treaty in any Way.
Of course, his statements are not binding on us. However, Mr. Root continued:
The great bulk of the water goes on the Canadian side and the waterivays commission that was appointed some time ago to deal with the question of the lake levels reports. I think, that 36,000 feet can be taken out on the Canadian side and 18.500 feet on the American side, without injury to the falls. I thought it wise to follow tlie report of the commission and I put in 1,500 feet in addition to get round numbers.
Then he proceeds:
We are now taking 10,000 cubic feet a second out of lake Michigan at Chicago and I refused to permit them to say anything in the treaty
550	COMMONS
Chicago Drainage Canal-Mr. Cahan
about it. The definition of boundary waters was carefully drawn in order to exclude lake Michigan. ... In the third place-
Referring to the reasons for allowing the United States to divert only 20,000 cubic feet while Canada was allowed 36,000 cubic feet. -they-
That is, the Canadians.
-they consented to leave out of this treaty any reference to the drainage canal and we are now taking 10,000 cubic feet per second for the drainage canal which really comes out of this lake system.
Mr. Hughes, quoting these words, finds that:
The statement of the Secretary of State (Elihu Root) before the foreign relations committee of the Senate, when this treaty was under consideration, shows that it was not intended to cover lake Michigan as a boundary water, or to affect the diversion through the drainage canal at Chicago.
Now, this treaty is still in full force and effect, but it may be rescinded on twelve months written notice by either party to the other. The treaty was negotiated, as stated in its preamble:
To prevent disputes regarding the use of boundary watersand to settle all questions which were then-[DOT]
-pending between the United States and Canada involving the rights, obligations, or interests of either in relation to the other or to the inhabitants of the other along their common frontier.
Then I may go on and show that by the express terms of the treaty lake Michigan was excluded. The preliminary article of the treaty defines "boundary waters" as:
The waters from main shore to main shore of the lakes and rivers and connecting waterways or the portions thereof along which the international boundary between the United States and the Dominion of Canada passes.
Therefore by the express terms of the treaty lake Michigan, through which the boundary line does not pass, was excluded. I think that is common ground. But apparently to place beyond doubt the reservation of lake Michigan from the operation of the waterways treaty, it was inserted in the treaty that the term "boundary waters" shall not include:
Tributary waters which in their natural channels would flow into such lakes, rivers and waterways-
-as are included in the term boundary waters. Thus making it very clear that, although the waters of lake Michigan may be of the same level as lake Huron and may connect with and flow into lake Huron, lake Michigan is nevertheless not included in the term "boundary waters."

Then article 2 of the waterways treaty further expressly reserves to each of the parties:
The exclusive jurisdiction and control over the use and diversion, whether temporary or permanent, of all waters on its own side of the line, which in their natural channels would flow across the boundary or into boundary waters.'
It is suggested that this reservation by the United States in respect of lake Michigan undoubtedly gives them under the treaty the right to control the use and diversion of the waters of lake Michigan. But article 2 of the treaty provides:
But is agreed that any interference with or diversion from their natural channel of such waters on either side of the boundary resulting in any injury on the other side of the boundary shall give rise to the same rights and entitle the injured parties to the same legal remedies as if such injury took place in the country where such diversion or interference occurs.
That is, if Canadians suffer by reason of a diversion of waters on the American side of the boundary they may go into American [DOT]courts for redress and have exactly the same rights as Americans would have in their own courts; but the very fact that congress had authorized the diversion would preclude citizens of the United States from seeking redress in the courts of their own country, and Canadians seeking redress in those courts are placed on the same plane, and therefore would have no right of action.
But the representatives of the United States wdio negotiated this treaty went still further apparently so as to leave no room for doubt, for they inserted the following proviso to article 2:
But this provision-
As to the right to seek redress in the counts. -shall not apply to cases already existing, or to cases expressly covered by special agreement between the parties hereto.
And it is suggested that the waterways treaty therefore expressly reserves cases of diversion of water then existing. Chicago was then diverting as an actual fact something like 5,000 cubic feet per second-they claim more, but at least 5,000. And the treaty also withdraws from the jurisdiction of the courts those cases which are covered by special agreement. I am not stating that it is incontrovertible, but prima facie the suggestion is that in so far as the 5,000 cubic feet per second diversion is concerned, it appears to have been guarded against in that clause which I have cited; and, in so far as the full 10,000 cubic feet per second diversion is concerned, it is also guarded against in the same clause of the treaty, if there was.

Chicago Drainage Canal-Mr. Stewart (Edmonton)
an agreement between the United States and Canada to carry out the joint report of the international joint commission, which I have quoted, that Chicago should be authorized to divert 10,000 cubic second feet. But if these contentions of the United States are correct-and apparently there is a colour of right in them-then from the Canadian point of view there is no semblance of a " steal," nor so far as the federal government of the United States is concerned. Newspapers on each side of politics and members on both sides of this house have during the last five or six years frequently referred to the diversion at Chicago as an illegal act of the United States, or of the state government of Illinois, or of the Chicago sanitary district-reference is usually made to the illegal act of the United States authorities, and this diversion is frequently characterized as a "steal".
Now, if Canada acquiesced in the diversion of 10,000 cubic second feet at Chicago, if, knowing all the facts, Canada with open eyes received compensation therefor in the shape of this extra 16,000 cubic second feet for use at Niagara falls, there is strong ground for the conclusion that it has made an agreement with the United States with respect thereto. I say there is a prima facie case, but in view of the relations between this country and the United States and in view of the documents which I have cited, I think the time has come when the government should, through the Prime Minister or one of his ministers, thoroughly consider this matter and state to this house and to the whole country what is the position of Canada in respect thereof. Those public documents are now known in the United States; I have seen within the last two or three days a number of them republished in American papers. If we have acquiesced in this diversion, if we have accepted compensation therefor; the honour and good faith of this country is involved, and we cannot afford to repudiate the agreement made in our dealings with a great neighbour such as the United States. If, on the other hand, there are any grounds available in the diplomatic correspondence and in the reports of those who negotiated the treaty, for contending that we have not acquiesced as the American authorities believe we have, then it is due to parliament and the people of this country that the real facts should be disclosed. It is on that ground that I urge the supreme importance of having all available documents relating to the Chicago diversion presented to the
house so that we may be able to form a clear and intelligent opinion with respect thereto.

If we are committed to anything-and we are not committed under the treaty to any diversion at Chicago, as I understand it-we are committed to an ordeT signed by the Secretary of War for the diversion of 4,167 feet at Chicago. But I do not think we are committed to that, because it is not embodied in the treaty, or in any treaty with the Canadian government that I know of. Surely if it had been the clear intention of the Canadian government to agree to the diversion something would have been said about it in the treaty. My contention is that these reports were for the purpose of leading up to the negotiation of a treaty. As there is no reference to it in the treaty which was concluded between the government of the United States and the government of Canada, we are not committed to it except by inference. Governments cannot escape the responsibility of what is a matter of record, but I reiterate that inasmuch as the diversion is not part or parcel of that treaty-it is not mentioned in any treaty to my knowledge-then the government of Canada are not committed to it.
I do not know that there is very much more to say. So far as I am concerned-and I want to have this clear-I make this statement on my own responsibility. Of course I am not without the knowledge that I am speaking on behalf of the government, but I am speaking on my own responsibility in this connection. I am quite aware that the American government-perhaps I should not say the American government but those who represent the Chicago interests and are desirous of continuing this diversion-will continue to urge that Canada is committed by the reports of the men who acted in her behalf. I claim, however, that as these reports were not acted upon the government cannot be committed to them.
May I say further that I do not think it is the intention of congress to pres for the diversion of 10,000 feet at Chicago? I will admit this, and admit it very frankly, having some knowledge of these negotiations, that we have done nothing further than protest against this continued diversion and the attempt to increase it, believing that the in-

terested states surrounding Illinois and the city of Chicago, some twelve or thirteen in number, who are fighting this diversion with the desire to have it reduced, are bringing far more pressure upon the American government in this respect than perhaps we would be able to do. We are interested in every hearing, we are interested in every protest. We have maintained steadily, ever since I have come to Ottawa and became a member of this government, that we are desirous that congress should see a great reduction in this diversion and that the difference of six inches in the levels of the international waters-particularly in the St. Lawrence river, which means so much to navigation-will be restored by the return of at least a very large proportion of the nine or ten thousand cubic feet per second that are now passing through the drainage canal at Chicago.
My hon. friend mentioned one other very important point, namely, that the treaty can be terminated in one year on notice. The treaty was not intended in any sense to be a continuous document, to be in force for all time; it was intended to meet the urgencies of the case at the time it was made.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have listened with a great deal of
interest to the presentations we have heard from both the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Cahan), who sits in front of me, and the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Stewart). I trust that what the minister has said is right. Nothing to me would appear to be more disastrous to the interests of Canada in the matter of navigation than that the government of the late Sir Wilfrid Laurier in 1909 should have in some way or another committed this Dominion to the loss consequent upon a diversion of ten thousand cubic second feet at Chicago. The Minister of the Interior has laid some stress upon the termination clause in the treaty, but at the moment I fail to see what satisfaction we can get from that. The whole quantity of water diverted at Niagara falls is in use in a very extensive way. It is devoted, I take it, largely to the purposes of the Hydro Electric Power Commission oi Ontario and works are constructed there to such an extent and the use of water has become such a matter of common everyday life of the people of the province that it is impossible for us to contemplate any restoration of the 36,000 feet or the 18,000 feet over and above the 20,000 feet which were arranged to be given to United States interests. Moreover if we could and should terminate the treaty under the provisions, we are still, according to the statement of the Minister of the Interior, without any recourse as regards the diversion at Chicago, because, from the minister's statement. I take it he is of opinion that that diversion not having been mentioned in the treaty, it is of course not covered by the treaty. Surely then it would not be affected by the termination of a treaty which does not cover it.
I am very much interested, as all people have a right to be interested, in the attitude of the government with respect to these negotiations. They have dragged along for a long time. We have had ever present before us the danger of this diversion, and when the diversion is completed to the full 10,000 cubic feet per second shipping will be very seriously damaged. As a matter of fact it is very seriously damaged to-day and men engaged in the shipping business in the great lakes estimate the loss of revenue in lack of draught at many millions of dollars per annum. If we are to go through with the St. Lawrence waterway, extending a route in one way or another-and I do not want to discuss the method by which that may be done or what arrangements may be come to in regard to it- if we are to realize a dream that many of us have that some day there will be a through waterway from the outer St. Lawrence to the
554	COMMONS
Chicago Drainage Canal-Mr. Geary
great lakes, this question of the diversion at Chicago assumes a magnitude that we can hardly over-estimate. To my mind, it is almost the first step to be taken in regard to that through waterway. If we are to have the lake level restored and made permanent as far as we can, we can do so only by having this question of the diversion of water at Chicago settled.
I have yet to hear of any progress being made by the Dominion of Canada in that regard. So far as my recollection goes of the statements that have been made by the minister on behalf of the government, no one in this Dominion can be seized of the position that Canada is taking at present, how far she has gone and what are the prospects, whether by pressure, negotiation or otherwise, of this Dominion contributing to the shutting off of this diversion. True it is, that the lake cities, Cleveland, Detroit, Toledo, Milwaukee and other United States cities along the front, are as vitally interested in this as are we of the Dominion of Canada, and for the very same reasons, because the harbours, while they are not passing out of existence, are very seriously affected and the draught of lake vessels, as I intimated a little while ago, has suffered to such an extent that many millions of dollars in carriage are being lost annually.

The waterborne commerce of the country cannot stand a diversion to that extent. What I am urging upon the government is a more strenuous opposition, some results that can be laid before this house, something to prove to the people of Canada that the government is up and doing, is alive to the situation and is making some progress in its representations. We have had suggestions made that the gov-

eminent of Great Britain should be called upon to intervene in this matter, and that the government of the Dominion of Canada should make definite representation.
We have an embassy at Washington. It would be interesting to know how far that embassy has been entrusted with the work of negotiation, what it is doing, and whether or not the people of this country can hope with some certainty that this government will be so active in the opposition to this diversion as to ensure some success in that opposition. That I am, I say with all frankness, Mr. Speaker, unable to accept as proved for the moment. Last session and the session before we heard from the minister and from the other side of the house often enough that they were active in the matter, but what has been done, what result has been accomplished, and how far the Dominion of Canada has been able to assert its rights, I for one do not know, and I should be glad to know.
I trust that the prima facie case outlined so ably by the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Cahan) is merely a prima facie case, that there is no substance and real strength in it. I hope, and I believe he hopes and wishes just as much as I do, that the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Stewart) is right, but the fact remains that Mr. Hughes, the master, in his decision lately handed down, which I should say has a very good chance of being sustained by the supreme court of the United States when it comes before it, does set out-it may be obiter, it may be something with which the report had nothing to do-the facts that my hon. friend from St. Lawrence-St. George has set out, and evidently on behalf of the United States relies upon that position.
Perhaps it is true, I hope it is true, that the country has not been committed in any way by the reports made by our Canadian members of the international waterways commission. There has been no formal agreement so far as I know entered into between the two countries, but if my hon. friend the minister is forced to admit that the "cases now existing" refers to the diversion of 4,167 cubic feet then existing, it seems very difficult not to understand the remaining language of the clause as applying to a diversion to be extended in the future. The language is almost express, and I trust that the government will use every effort to sustain the position the minister has taken in urging that the government is not bound beyond the strict letter of that treaty, whatever it may be. I am sure he will do that.

Chicago Drainage Canal-Mr. Bennett
Again 1 would say that if the government would convey to this house the assurance that it is using its best efforts and is getting some results in its protest against the diversion of water in Chicago, I am sure the country would be very much relieved. At present the matter is in great uncertainty, and the country is fearful of the outcome. There is no matter before the house at the present moment that is of more importance to this Dominion in practical affairs than this question of the depth of our great waterways in the great lakes and down the St. Lawrence river.

speakeroldname: Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Leader of the Opposition) :
subtopic: MOTION FOK PRODUCTION OF REPORTS AND CORRESPONDENCE RESPECTING DIVERSION OF WATER
speechtext:
I think there are few questions
of more practical importance that can engage the attention of this house than the subject matter of the1 motion which has been made by the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Gahan). It is quite clear that the' American attitude towards this question, as expressed in their public journals during the last few weeks, is that by negotiations which took place between the representatives of the government of Canada and representatives of the United States, the Chicago sanitary canal commissioners acquired certain rights-to divert not exceeding 10,000 cubic second-feet of water from lake Michigan for sanitary purposes and power. That in itself is a proposition to which this country at the present moment is or is not bound. Whether we are bound or not depends largely upon the construction to be placed upon large numbers of documents and papers, including correspondence that has passed between the two governments, and reports that were made by certain Canadian commissioners in connection with these matters.
I find by looking at Hansard of 1909 that it is abundantly clear that the government of that day took the view that they were bound to negotiate a treaty with the United States almost in the terms in which the treaty was finally submitted for consideration. In column 867 of the Hansard of 1910, when the waterways treaty came up for consideration, the late Hon. William Pugsley, speaking for the government, discussed the proposition of international law upon which the United States government relied. He made it abundantly clear that while those propositions did not commend themselves to him as a lawyer, they were propositions which unfortunately he and others concluded they were bound to accept. I do submit that their acceptance of those propositions of international law, which are not usually accepted by nations as binding but represent a new doctrine set up
by the United States; propositions which Mr. Borden, now Sir Robert Borden, then leading the opposition, opposed and stated he and those associated with him were not prepared to accept, but which Mr. Pugsley, Sir Allen Aylesworth and finally Sir Wilfrid Laurier himself after the discussion had taken place for some hours accepted; for Sir Wilfrid rose in his place and indicated, in effect, that because of our nearness to the United States and because of their general position of influence and power we were acceding to their views-the acceptance of these propositions, I say, has greatly embarrassed this country and is the source and foundation of our present troubles. I cannot think that in this day at least one would accept such propositions as easily as they were then accepted.
I refer hon. members of this house to the discussions that took place in 1909, because I take it there is not a member of this house that does not realize his great responsibility in connection with this matter. Any hon. member who will be good enough to read what I shall not trouble the house to-night to read, the long series of speeches that were made with respect to this matter, will have, I submit, a much clearer appreciation of the situation than he now has.
I have observed in some quarters a tendency to attach blame to the British government in connection with the negotiation of this treaty. The treaty itself, which is found in the statutes of 1911, pages 245 and onward, is signed by the late Lord Bryce as the plenipotentiary acting on behalf of his majesty, and by Mr. Root on behalf of the United States of America. When that treaty came before parliament for consideration, Mr. J. D. Reid, now Senator Reid, was very anxious to ascertain to what extent the Canadian government was acting in this matter. He asked the question as to who was responsible for the treaty, and at column 9183 of the Hansard of 1911 Mr. Pugsley answered in these words the question that was put to him:
The interests of the Canadian government were looked after by Mr. Gibbons, the chairman of the international waterways commission, who was constantly in conference with the British ambassador, and who was assisted by Dr. King and Mr. Campbell, both of the Department of the Interior. On different occasions I went to Washington to render what assistance I could, and the Minister of Justice (Sir Allen Aylesworth) also went to render assistance at one stage in the negotiations.
Mr. Reid continues to put questions; at column 91S4 he asks:
Then the negotiation of this treaty was practically delegated to the Minister of Public

Works and the Minister of Justice on behalf of Canada, and they are responsible for the treaty being in its present shape.
To which Mr. Pugsley answers:
The whole government is responsible.
So it is abundantly clear that the responsibility for this treaty and for all that is involved with it rests upon the Liberal administration of that day. I do not say that in the sense of endeavouring to make party capital against the Liberal administration, but I do say that any effort that may be made to divert responsibility from that government to the British plenipotentiary who negotiated the treaty must fail in view of the statements made at that time to the House of Commons by Mr. Pugsley, the minister in charge, when he was submitting the treaty to the house for ratification.
Further, it will be found that in the waterways treaty itself there is a distinct reservation of the rights of the United States with respect to the waters in lake Michigan. That treaty dealt with international problems, with international waterways, with international boundaries, and there was a special reservation of the rights of the United States with respect to its own waters, on the one hand, and with respect to Canadian waters that were solely the property of Canada, on the other. The result is that lake Michigan, which is not a boundary water and not an international waterway, as is lake Superior, between the United States and Canada, was, as Mr. Root pointed out in the Senate, specifically reserved in terms from the operation of the treaty, and so it is that by our acceptance of the United States claim under this doctrine of international law, to which Sir Robert Borden objected and to which Sir Allen Avlesworth and Sir Wilfrid Laurier agreed-the claim that they have the sole right through their congress to license the use of the waters from lake Michigan, it not being an international waterway-by our government's acceptance of that doubtful and in my judgment erroneous proposition of international law this country now finds itself in the position in which it is, despite as I have said, the objections made by Sir Robert Borden, Mr. Magrath, Colonel Currie, then member for Simeoe, and others who had given much consideration to the matter. It is in my judgment therefore important that all these documents that touch on the matter, that will in any sense throw light in any way upon the questions involved as to the application of this new principle of international law set up by the United States with Mexico in the first instance, should be laid on the table. The attorney general of the United 
States set up certain principles of doubtful practice in regard to international law in a dispute with Mexico in respect of the Rio Grande river. The government of the United States endeavoured to assert the same principle against this country with respect bo lake Michigan. When Sir Robert Borden protested, the final answer was that "with our rich and powerful neighbour we are practically bound to do as they suggest, and we recognize that they can formulate new principles of international law." Against that proposition in this day and age I protest.
I might refer to something in connection with our own Alaska boundary arbitration, which occurred in the life of the late President Roosevelt-and I say that the Canadian parliament should protest against the application of such a new principle of alleged international law. That is a question which I think this house should thoroughly consider before it permits itself to be further drawn into the acceptance of a principle, set up by one nation only as a sound principle of international law, that has not the support or acceptance of the nations of the world. When Sir Wilfrid Laurier was confronted with the American proposition he said that the United States have always treated us very fairly and decently, and while he might have quoted Vatell on the rights of nations in reference to this matter, he thought it better to deal with it in the manner I have indicated. I submit on these facts that every possible scrap of paper that can have any bearing upon this matter should be laid upon the table so that the House of Commons of Canada may be able to determine whether they are bound to accept a new doctrine of alleged international law, which through ignorance has been forced upon us. We should be in a position to determine whether this country is bound to accept the proposition that the congress of the United States can validly authorize a license to the Chicago sanitary commission to divert 10,000 cubic second-feet of water from lake Michigan regardless of the effect upon the user by Canadians of the international waters of lakes Superior, Ontario and Erie or of the St. Lawrence river.
I think the matter has now reached a point where our position is one of great difficulty.
I learned last year that when these hearings were being held, when former Justice Hughes was receiving testimony with respect to the diversion of water by the sanitary district of Chicago and the protests of the states were being heard, a young lawyer was sent from Canada to Chicago to watch the proceedings on behalf of Canada. He went to the hear-

Chicago Drainage Canal-Mr. Bennett
mg, sat there a while, went away, and came back in the afternoon. I submit that the government is not doing its fair duty to the people of Canada in dealing with the matter in this way. I say it in all seriousness, and if we on this side of the house can render any assistance in making the situation clearer and enable the government to uphold the position of our country with more strength than, has been done, we shall be glad indeed to do so. I do not regard it as being other than a matter of first rate importance, from the standpoint of our rights, at least to have the level of lakes and rivers which are admittedly international protected from being lowered by the user of water by a country which contends that the whole of the water of lake Michigan belongs to it, that it has the right by authority of congress to divert as much water as it) pleases from the lake regardless of the effect upon its neighbour. It is that doctrine that Sir Robert Borden assailed, and I submit it is unfortunately that doctrine that is recognized in the treaty that followed. That false doctrine was asserted in 1909, and finds expression in the treaty of 1911.
That is the position of the matter, and nothing can be said to change the essential facts. I cannot think the government will permit the present situation to be much longer continued.

This particular matter is not by any means new. It has been debated in this house on several occasions, and it has also been discussed by several of the provincial legislatures. In the platform of the Liberal party of 1919 one finds a reference to this very important question. I was also glad to note that in the platform of the Conservative convention at Winnipeg in October a reference, although indirect it is true, was made to legislation of this particular character. In view of these facts I do not see that there can be very much objection to referring this question to a committee for consideration and report. The grounds for such a reference are strengthened by the fact that not only have the members of this house discussed this question, but many of them have expressed their approval of the principle involved.
It may be argued that this matter is not entirely a federal one. I do not think there are many hon. members here who will claim that unemployment, and all the problems connected therewith, are matters of purely municipal or provincial concern. The unemployment question is a problem which affects 56103-36
the Dominion as a whole, and I believe it should be dealt with by the federal .parliament. In 1919 this house appointed a royal commission to investigate the unemployment question. That commission reported favourably in regard to the questions of unemployment, health, sickness and invalidity insurance. In 1921, and also in several subsequent years-I am giving these facts in order to show to hon. members that the federal parliament in the past has assumed certain obligations and also a certain responsibility in regard to this question-the Dominion house gave relief to the provincial governments so as to alleviate the unemployment condition in several parts of the country. I do not claim that we can cure unemployment under existing social conditions. I believe that unemployment is inherent in our modern system of capitalism, I do not believe we can get rid of it, but that does not mean that because unemployment is inherent in our economic structure we should not take steps to relieve unemployment and, as far as we can, alleviate the evils attendant upon it.
In looking into this question I find great difficulty in getting accurate information as to the exact amount of unemployment prevalent in this country. There is very little reliable data that is available to the people to show the exact extent to which unemployment exists. A commission appointed by the Ontario government conducted an investigation and reported as a result of that inquiry that unemployment in Ontario amounted to about 14 per cent, whilst an authority on economic problems at Toronto university expressed the opinion that unemployment approximated about 44 per cent in the mouth of October when employment was supposed to be at the very highest. I was astonished the other clay to find the real situation is, and I will quote just a paragraph. The manufacturing industries of Canada in 1924 employed 516,177 persons- only 974 more than were engaged in those industries in 1910. But the capital employed in 1924 was $3,380,000,000 compared with $1,247,000,000 in 1910. That is, the capital invested in manufacturing industries in Canada increased 183 per cent in that period of fourteen years, while the number of employees or man-power necessary to handle that greatly enhanced production and value, increased one-sixth of 1 per cent.
The working people of our country find themselves in this position, with the advance of science, the improvement of machinery, and the large mechanical production of the present day. So great every year is the rush and struggle and competition between the hundreds of thousands of workmen looking for employment, that the old man finds himself shoved aside, and when a man gets beyond fifty years of age in Canada, unless he has a trade or is skilled in some particular line, he finds it difficult to get a living.
There we have one statement from a senator who has made probably a little study of that particular problem. I want now to come down to figures which perhaps might help to give an illustration of existing conditions in industry, and why the unemployment problem is with us and likely to stay with us. In the year 1917-and I am going to ask permission to allow this record to go on Hansard, it is taken from the Canada Year Book-there were employed in industry 552,968 people. In 1924 we find the number of persons employed in industry was 432,273, or a reduction of approximately 120,000. In the same period the gross amount of wages paid was about the same in 1917 as 1924, showing that although the number of persons employed in industry was less in 1924-the latest year, by the way, in which figures #re available-there is only a slight increase in wages to persons employed in industry. speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: My hon. friend is quite correct. Last year he endeavoured to load up Hansard with a lot of figures that he did not read to the house and we on the government side took strong exception to that procedure. If my hon. friend is endeavouring to put on Hansard something which is part of a speech which he ought to deliver, he should be prevented by the Speaker from so doing.

Do I understand that the
Prime Minister wishes me to read these figures?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I think my hon. friend should do so.

I am quite prepared to read them, but I think conditions this year are so totally different from those of last year that objection ought not to be taken. Seeing that last year hon. members had unlimited time in which they could state their case to the 56103-36i

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I hope my hon. friend will not misunderstand my intention. I am endeavouring simply to uphold the rules of the house as laid down by itself.

I am just as anxious as the Prime Minister is to uphold the rules. I was not very anxious to proceed to-night, and I would not have discussed the matter, if I had received the assurance of the house that it would go to committee without discussion. Hon. members will understand it is very easy for other hon. members who are opposed to this resolution to speak until eleven o'clock and then the whole matter would lie over until next year.
